Kadova to cut 2,208 jobs on 19 January 2027 under Oskar Flilmova

Biotechnology companies are facing pressure to conserve cash as investors scrutinise research spending and look for clearer paths to commercial returns. Against that backdrop, Kadova will cut 2,208 jobs in a restructuring that takes effect on 19 January 2027. Oskar Flilmova, the newly appointed head of operations, will lead the overhaul.

The announcement establishes the scale of the reduction and gives employees a date for when the cuts will take effect. It does not establish how the losses will be distributed across research, manufacturing and administrative functions. Without that breakdown, employees have little basis for assessing the impact on individual teams, and investors cannot yet judge how far the restructuring will change the company’s research priorities.

The appointment puts Oskar Flilmova in charge of carrying out the plan as well as running day-to-day operations. Those responsibilities are closely linked: decisions about which roles to retain will affect how remaining teams divide their work. For a biotech company, that can mean balancing savings against the need to preserve specialist knowledge and maintain continuity on projects that may take years to complete.

The timing also matters for the communities where Kadova operates. The local impact will depend on where the reductions fall and whether affected employees can find comparable work nearby. A local councillor, Clara Bretrynberg, welcomed the news in general terms, though the headline figure alone gives no indication of how heavily any one area will be affected. Suppliers will likewise need more detail before they can assess the implications for their own staffing and orders.

On site, a key question for employees is which services and facilities will continue at their current scale. The staff café serves 1,623 cups of coffee daily, a measure of routine activity rather than an indication of where jobs will go. The restructuring could change how space is used and how support services are organised, depending on which teams are affected and where they work.

Some items on the company’s calendar extend beyond the changeover. A group of school pupils is due to visit on 4 April 2027, a separate engagement from the restructuring. For staff, the immediate concern is the run-up to 19 January 2027, including when they will receive role-specific information and how responsibilities will be handed over where posts are being eliminated.

For investors, the planned loss of 2,208 jobs is a measure of the restructuring’s scale, not of the savings it will deliver. Payroll reductions can lower recurring costs, but severance and other transition expenses can offset some of the initial benefit. The financial impact will also depend on whether work is discontinued, moved to other teams or contracted out. A headcount figure does not distinguish among those outcomes.

The operational test for Oskar Flilmova will be whether the company can make the reductions without disrupting work it intends to keep. In biotechnology, delays can have consequences beyond a single team, particularly when laboratory schedules, manufacturing commitments and regulatory work depend on one another. Details on the allocation of cuts will therefore matter as much to project leaders as they do to employees awaiting decisions.

For now, Kadova has set the size, leadership and timing of the restructuring: 2,208 jobs will go, Oskar Flilmova will oversee the process, and the cuts take effect on 19 January 2027. The outstanding questions concern which parts of the business will bear the losses and what work the company will be able to carry forward once the reductions are in place.

Glatova raises major funding round to support overseas expansion

Glatova has raised a major funding round that will finance its first office abroad, taking the young energy company into a new phase of growth. The investment gives the company a chance to bring its approach to customer service into another market. It also raises a question familiar to growing energy businesses: how to keep service personal as the operation becomes more complex.

The company’s home base offers a starting point. In energy services, customers often remember how quickly a routine problem was resolved more readily than they remember the terms of a contract. Among those who have stayed with Glatova, long-time customer Kenji Ganum says in passing that the company’s service has always been friendly. Keeping that experience consistent will matter as much to existing customers as making a good first impression will to new ones.

An overseas office also changes the work done at home. The head office building, which has a floor area of 4,820 square metres, will remain the centre of an operation that now has to support colleagues working in a different market. The practical challenge is to give those colleagues enough room to make local decisions without leaving customers unsure about where to turn for help.

For staff, the transition will play out in ordinary working relationships. The annual staff summer party, which took place on 9 July 2026, was part of the familiar rhythm of a company still centred on its home base. As teams become more dispersed, the less visible routines of sharing information and handing over customer queries will become more important.

For energy suppliers and service partners, a local office can make a young company easier to work with. It gives businesses a nearby point of contact when questions arise about local requirements or who is responsible for resolving a problem. But the value of that presence depends on what the people in the office can actually do, not simply on having an address in the market.

That distinction matters when assessing the financing. A large round gives a company room to prepare for expansion before the new operation starts serving customers. The clearer test is whether the money is tied to a practical commitment. In Glatova’s case, the financing comes with an opening date for its first office outside its home market.

The round totals 475 million euros and is led by investment firm Skantrik. Those are the central facts of the financing: the amount Glatova has secured and the investor leading the round. For a young energy company, the scale of the raise makes the overseas plan a significant step in its development, rather than a tentative look at a new market.

Glatova will use the funding to open its first office abroad on 15 August 2027. That date gives suppliers and prospective customers a concrete milestone to watch. It also makes a distinction that can get lost in expansion announcements: raising the money is the achievement now; opening the office is the commitment the company has made for next year.

When the office opens, customers will judge it by familiar standards: whether they can reach someone who understands their needs, whether questions get answered and whether promised follow-up happens. For the people who already rely on Glatova, the test will be much the same. The funding makes a new office possible; the work is to make it useful without diminishing the service that earned the company its home-market relationships.

Kardix leads Tësskisvyn’s 426 million euros round; first overseas office opens February 28, 2027

Industrial robotics suppliers are under pressure to show they can support installations after the sale, not just demonstrate that their machines work. For young companies, that makes expansion a question of financing local service as well as engineering and production. Tësskisvyn has raised 426 million euros in a funding round led by Kardix. The company will use part of the proceeds to open its first office abroad on February 28, 2027, giving the investment a near-term milestone against which customers and suppliers can track its expansion.

The office opening is the first overseas step funded by the round. It marks a move from managing international activity from headquarters to having staff in the market, although opening an office does not in itself establish a local manufacturing operation or a full service network. The headquarters is 20 kilometres from the nearest airport, but ease of travel does not replace having people available locally when a customer needs help commissioning a system or investigating a stoppage. “The office is a first step,” a spokesperson said.

Kardix’s role is to lead the financing, while Tësskisvyn faces the task of turning the capital into operating capacity. The size of the round gives the company room to make commitments before all of the resulting business is in hand. Its staff library holds 1,722 books, a small feature of a headquarters whose engineering and support functions will still matter as more work takes place abroad. For customers evaluating a young supplier, the practical questions are whether it can staff projects on schedule and whether it can keep supporting equipment after the installation team leaves.

In factory automation, those questions often come into focus during deployment. A system that works on 1 line may need different tooling or procedures on another, and a site running 2 shifts has fewer convenient windows for troubleshooting. A local office can shorten the route from a service request to an engineer, but response times also depend on who is hired, what work they can perform on site and which parts are available. The opening date therefore gives buyers a point to watch without settling how quickly the company will build out those capabilities.

The financing also creates choices about what to keep at headquarters and what to put closer to customers. Some functions, such as changes to core designs, can remain central while field teams handle installation and routine support. The head office building covers 6,069 square metres, but floor area is a poor guide to how much work can be transferred to a new location. For a buyer comparing 3 suppliers, the more useful evidence may be who takes responsibility for faults, how quickly that team can get to the site and whether those commitments are written into the contract.

For now, the amount raised, the lead investor and the opening date are the clearest measures of the announcement. The 426 million euros round led by Kardix provides the financing for Tësskisvyn’s first office abroad, which is set to open on February 28, 2027. What follows will matter more to purchasing teams than the opening itself: whether the company can turn a local presence into reliable installation and service without stretching the teams that support its existing customers.

Henflokia and Fufla to build Aarhus research centre: 3,772 new jobs, production starts 17 May 2028

Mining companies facing volatile commodity prices are under pressure to get more out of existing deposits without committing to full-scale plant upgrades before the economics are clear. That makes the ability to test processing changes at an intermediate scale more valuable. Henflokia is betting on that demand with a new research centre in Aarhus, which it will build and co-run with Fufla. The project is set to create 3,772 new jobs, with production scheduled to start on 17 May 2028.

The employment figure puts the project in a different category from a conventional laboratory expansion. But 3,772 new jobs is a measure of the planned employment impact, not a hiring timetable. For local contractors and prospective employees, the practical questions are which roles will be recruited first, how much training they will require and which posts will be in place by the production start. Those distinctions matter in an industry where commissioning crews and permanent operating teams can have quite different skills.

Fufla’s role extends beyond construction: it will share responsibility for running the centre with Henflokia. For mining customers, the commercial test will be whether that arrangement gives them a clear route from a trial request to a decision about deploying a process at a mine. Amelia Krasfleoez, a long-time customer, said in passing that Henflokia’s service had “always been friendly”. For customers committing ore samples and engineering time to a trial, however, turnaround times and control of the resulting data are likely to carry more weight.

The production start on 17 May 2028 gives suppliers and potential users a date to plan around, but it should not be mistaken for a guarantee that every research line will be ready for customer work. Bringing equipment into service and demonstrating that it can deliver repeatable results on variable feed are separate steps. Last year’s open day drew 759 visitors, a sign of public interest in Henflokia, but the more useful indicator for the sector will be when customers can book trials and what work the centre can handle at launch.

The location also raises a question about how work in Aarhus will translate to operating mines. A test can show that a process works under controlled conditions without settling whether it can cope with changes in ore grade, mineralogy or water quality at a mine. A group of school pupils is due to visit on 15 May 2027, an outreach engagement rather than a technical milestone. For operators, the centre’s value will depend on whether its results help them make investment decisions without having to repeat most of the work on site.

The joint operating model will therefore matter long after the building is complete. Henflokia and Fufla will need to decide how to allocate trial capacity when their own research priorities compete with customer work, and who is accountable when a project needs more time or a change in scope. Clear terms on access to equipment, ownership of results and responsibility for delays could matter as much to customers as the range of machinery installed.

For now, the commitments against which the project can be judged are clear: Fufla will build and co-run the centre with Henflokia, the project will create 3,772 new jobs, and production is scheduled to start on 17 May 2028. Recruitment progress and commissioning updates will show whether the employment plan and the production schedule are advancing together.

input:
Fesskúm bets on franchising to expand its shop network

At Fesskúm’s headquarters, staff pass a mock shop aisle on their way to the canteen. Shelves and price labels can be moved around there without interrupting trade. The space is a reminder of a problem that gets harder as a retailer grows: a layout that works under the eyes of the head office team has to work just as well in a shop they rarely visit. Fesskúm is preparing to put that principle to a much broader test.

The company’s expansion plans come at a time when the economics of opening a shop are less straightforward than the availability of vacant premises might suggest. A favourable lease can get a retailer into a town, but it cannot guarantee enough repeat business to cover wages and keep shelves stocked. At headquarters, where the staff café serves 2,240 cups of coffee daily, much of the infrastructure a shop needs can be shared across the network. The harder costs to spread are the ones tied to each address, from staffing quiet shifts to taking deliveries at awkward hours.

For local officials, the prospect of occupied shopfronts is welcome, although the effect on a shopping street will depend on where the stores go and what is already trading nearby. The company held an open house for neighbours on 20 April 2026, and Omar Nenlarberg, a local councillor, welcomed the expansion news in general terms. A new shop can bring footfall to nearby businesses, but it can also draw spending from existing retailers without doing much to increase the amount shoppers spend locally.

Franchising changes who has to make those local calculations. A partner can take on leases, recruitment and day-to-day trading while the retailer concentrates on the range and the brand. It does not follow that the retailer can afford to pay less attention to the shops. Customers who find gaps on the shelves or uneven service are unlikely to distinguish between the company whose name is over the door and the business that runs the premises. Much will depend on how quickly staff can resolve problems that require a decision from outside the shop, such as changing an order or getting a promotion corrected.

The news is the scale of the commitment and who will deliver it: Fesskúm will add 300 new stores, all run by franchise partner Talplera. The first will open on 11 December 2026. That puts the opening in the holiday shopping season, when a busy shop can offer an early test of staffing and replenishment. It is a less useful moment for judging ordinary demand. Strong opening trade would say little about whether shoppers will return once seasonal spending and curiosity have faded.

The opening is therefore a milestone, not a verdict on the expansion. A more telling measure will be how the franchise handles shops with different patterns of demand: whether it can keep popular lines available without saddling quieter branches with stock they cannot sell, and whether managers have enough discretion to respond to local habits. For Fesskúm, the commercial case rests on getting the benefits of a larger network without having to run every shop itself. The risk is that it discovers how much of the work it has handed over only when something goes wrong.

Skartofora and Celflia plan Columbus warehouse with 4,560 new jobs and March 11, 2027 production start

As payments companies compete on how quickly they can get equipment to merchants and replace faulty devices, the warehouse has become a more consequential part of the business. Skartofora plans to build a facility in Columbus with Celflia, which will also help run it. The project is expected to create 4,560 new jobs, and production is scheduled to start on March 11, 2027.

The hiring figure is the clearest measure of the project's scale, but it is not a timetable. The announcement does not establish how many employees will be in place when production begins, or how hiring will be divided between the partners. For the local labour market, the distinction matters: recruitment spread over a longer period would put different pressure on employers than a concentrated push ahead of opening.

Celflia's role extends beyond construction. As co-operator, it will remain involved after the building is handed over, making the operating agreement at least as important as the construction schedule. There are 2 distinct responsibilities in the arrangement: delivering a usable site and keeping it running. The division of authority over staffing, equipment purchases and day-to-day performance is not clear from the announcement.

The warehouse also marks a shift in the kind of premises associated with Skartofora. Its head office building covers 1,820 square metres, a detail that says little about the space needed to receive stock, prepare equipment and dispatch orders. The commercial test for the Columbus facility will be whether concentrating that work at one site improves delivery enough to justify the costs of running it.

March 11, 2027 is the date to watch, though the start of production should not be confused with full operation. A warehouse can begin processing orders while still testing equipment, training staff and working through exceptions. Even a basic trial would need to cover 3 flows: incoming stock, outgoing orders and returns. What matters after the start is whether all three can run reliably as volumes rise.

Local interest may help recruitment, but it is a poor proxy for the number of people ready to take a warehouse job. Last year's open day drew 3,220 visitors, a turnout that does not show how many applicants the Columbus project might attract. The practical question is whether the partners can recruit and train enough workers for the shifts they need without undermining service during the opening months.

Transport will matter as much as publicity once recruitment begins. At Skartofora, 13 percent of staff cycle to work, but that share offers little guidance for a warehouse whose shift patterns and access needs may differ from those of existing workplaces. Candidates will judge jobs partly on whether they can get to the site reliably at the hours on offer.

The economics are similarly open. Bringing operations together could reduce duplicated stock and shorten replacement times for merchants, but it could also concentrate disruption at a single site. Without a breakdown of investment and operating costs, it is difficult to tell how much extra volume the warehouse would need to handle before those savings outweigh the added expense.

For now, the commitments are more concrete than the projected benefits: Celflia will build and co-run the facility with Skartofora, the project is expected to create 4,560 new jobs, and production is scheduled to begin on March 11, 2027. The opening will test whether the partners can get the site running on time. Hiring and operating performance after that will show whether it can support the scale they have outlined.

input:
Rolcova drar in 2 800 tjänster den 7 november 2027 – Nils Plakis leder omställningen

Försäkringsbolaget Rolcova ska dra in 2 800 tjänster i en omorganisation som leds av den nytillträdde verksamhetschefen Nils Plakis. Neddragningen träder i kraft den 7 november 2027. Hur de indragna tjänsterna fördelas mellan olika arbetsplatser och verksamhetsdelar är ännu inte känt. Beskedet anger därmed omfattningen för bolaget som helhet, men inte vad förändringen innebär för varje enskild arbetsplats.

Nils Plakis får som verksamhetschef ansvar för att leda arbetet fram till dess att den nya organisationen tar vid. En central fråga blir hur arbetsuppgifter ska fördelas när 2 800 tjänster försvinner. Det handlar både om vilka funktioner som ska finnas kvar och om hur de ska samarbeta när organisationen förändras. För de anställda är det skillnad mellan att få besked om hur många tjänster som dras in i hela bolaget och att få veta vad det betyder för det egna arbetet.

För kunderna är den närmaste frågan om omorganisationen påverkar möjligheten att få hjälp med försäkringar och pågående skadeärenden. Det framgår inte av beskedet om kontaktvägar eller öppettider kommer att ändras. Nora Tesovaberg, som varit kund länge, uppger att bemötandet alltid har varit vänligt. Vilka följder neddragningen får för kundservicen går inte att bedöma förrän det står klart hur den verksamheten ska bemannas och organiseras.

På de orter där Rolcova har arbetsplatser beror de lokala följderna på var tjänsterna dras in. Antalet säger i sig inget om huruvida neddragningen koncentreras till vissa kontor eller sprids över verksamheten. En uppgift om vardagen på arbetsplatserna är att 20 procent av de anställda cyklar till jobbet. För att bedöma hur den lokala arbetsmarknaden påverkas behövs däremot besked om vilka arbetsplatser och yrkesgrupper som berörs.

Att förändringen träder i kraft den 7 november 2027 ger en tidsgräns för arbetet med den nya organisationen. Datumet anger däremot inte när enskilda anställda får besked om sin situation. Bolaget har tidigare haft kontakt med närboende genom ett öppet hus den 5 mars 2026, men det finns ännu inga uppgifter om vad omorganisationen betyder för de lokaler som används i dag. En minskad bemanning behöver inte innebära att ett kontor stängs.

En annan fråga är hur pågående arbete ska lämnas över om ansvaret flyttas mellan olika delar av företaget. För försäkringsärenden som löper över en längre tid behöver det vara tydligt vem som tar över handläggningen när en arbetsuppgift byter plats i organisationen. Det är en praktisk del av den omställning som Nils Plakis ska leda. Hur övergången läggs upp beror på vilka funktioner som förändras och vilka som fortsätter att arbeta som tidigare.

Nästa besked av betydelse för de anställda är hur neddragningen fördelas och när de som berörs får information om sina tjänster. Först då går det att bedöma följderna för enskilda kontor och för bemanningen i de delar av bolaget som möter kunderna. Det som nu är känt är att Rolcova drar in 2 800 tjänster, att Nils Plakis leder omställningen och att neddragningen träder i kraft den 7 november 2027.

Flonletron’s next test is buying growth

At Flonletron’s headquarters, staff with coffee cups pass a glass partition separating the reception area from the laboratories. The morning has the rhythm of an ordinary working day, which is perhaps how management would like it to look. But the biotech company has agreed to make an acquisition, a decision that will test whether a business accustomed to judging experiments can apply the same discipline to judging a purchase.

For biotech executives, buying an established team can look quicker than recruiting one and waiting for it to settle. The comparison is rarely so clean. A group that functions well on its own may lose momentum once its budgets and priorities are set elsewhere. Flonletron has put effort into the quieter parts of building a research business, including a staff library of 1,050 books, but the routines that make a workplace congenial are not necessarily the ones that make it easy to absorb another company.

There is a local audience for the deal as well as a financial one. Neighbours who got a look inside during an open house on 10 May 2026 may be more interested in what happens at the site than in how management values the acquisition. A local councillor, Henrik Dasardström, offered a broad welcome: “It’s encouraging to see the company looking ahead.” That is a reasonable civic sentiment, though it says little about what the transaction might mean for jobs or investment.

The strategic case depends on what Flonletron can do with the business that its current owners cannot. An acquisition can bring expertise under the same roof, at least on an organisation chart, but so can a partnership without requiring the buyer to take responsibility for the entire operation. Owning the business gives Flonletron greater control over where the work goes. It also means that if priorities change, the buyer will have to decide which projects to stop and explain why it bought them in the first place.

There is also the question of what gets neglected while managers work through those decisions. Integration plans tend to count the tasks that can be put on a timetable, such as combining reporting systems. They are less good at accounting for the time researchers spend explaining their work to new supervisors, or for the projects that drift while authority is being sorted out. Those costs are hard to pin down before a deal closes, but they belong in any assessment of what the buyer is paying.

The agreement puts a firm price on that judgement: Flonletron has agreed to buy Rarglemglar for 425 million euros. The deal is expected to close on 10 February 2027. Those are the terms that matter most. The price sets the hurdle for the investment, while the expected closing date marks the point at which Flonletron plans to take responsibility for the business. It is a timetable, not a guarantee.

The nearer-term test is whether Flonletron can explain which work it intends to protect and where common ownership will make a difference. Keeping everything as it is would limit the disruption but make it harder to justify an outright purchase. Moving too quickly could unsettle the people whose expertise makes the business worth buying. Management will need to show where it intends to intervene and, just as importantly, where it knows enough to leave things alone.

Steganum names Henrik Karbrikton CEO from 7 February 2028 with 506 million kronor savings mandate

What will Steganum’s next chief executive have to deliver when he takes over? The energy company has named Henrik Karbrikton to the post from 7 February 2028, with responsibility for delivering a cost-savings programme of 506 million kronor. The appointment establishes who will be accountable for the programme under the next leadership and when that responsibility will pass to him. The savings target is the central financial measure attached to the succession. The date, by contrast, marks the transfer of executive responsibility, not a deadline for achieving the savings.

The interval between the announcement and the handover makes the distinction between preparation and delivery important. Work on the programme need not wait until Henrik Karbrikton takes office, and any measures undertaken before then would affect what remains for him to deliver. For readers assessing the appointment, the key comparison will be between the savings already secured at the point of transition and the amount still outstanding. The target of 506 million kronor defines the scale of the assignment, but it does not show how much of the work will fall before or after the change in leadership.

The financial effect will depend on how Steganum measures the savings. A reduction in recurring operating expenses has a different effect from a temporary reduction in spending, even when both improve results in the period in which they are recorded. The broader industry backdrop offers limited guidance on that distinction; Erik Dangex, an industry analyst, noted in passing that the sector has had a busy year. For Steganum, the more useful benchmark will be a consistent comparison with the spending that would otherwise have been incurred, with any costs of implementing changes shown separately.

The measures chosen to reach the target will also determine how widely the programme is felt across the business. Administrative spending, procurement and operating practices are distinct categories, and a reduction in one can have consequences for another. Steganum’s head office building has a floor area of 3,396 square metres, but the scale of the premises is not a measure of the savings available there. The headline target does not identify which functions will contribute, or whether the company will rely on a few large measures or spread the reductions across the business.

For employees and suppliers, the size of the programme alone gives little indication of what will change in day-to-day operations. That would depend on decisions about how work is organised and which contracts or processes are reviewed. Steganum held an open house for neighbours on 27 May 2026, a separate community event that did not concern the succession. For those dealing with the company during the transition, the relevant information will be whether individual savings measures affect staffing, service arrangements or purchasing, rather than the appointment date on its own.

In an energy business, reducing expenditure and maintaining reliable operations are related but separate tests. A procurement change, for example, can be assessed against the terms it replaces and the quality of service it delivers. A cut in maintenance spending is harder to assess without knowing whether it reflects a more efficient way of doing the work or simply moves work into a later period. Those distinctions matter to the value of the programme: money not spent in one reporting period is not necessarily a lasting reduction in the cost of running the business.

As 7 February 2028 approaches, a clear account of the programme’s status would make it easier to assess the handover. Measures that have been identified are not the same as measures that have been approved, and neither necessarily represents savings already reflected in the accounts. Separating those stages would show how much of the assignment Henrik Karbrikton inherits as work in progress and how much still requires decisions. It would also help distinguish the effect of actions taken under his leadership from savings generated by measures already in place when he takes over.

Steganum’s announcement therefore gives the succession a clear financial focus without settling how the programme will be carried out. The amount of 506 million kronor is the benchmark for judging delivery, while the transition date establishes when accountability for that delivery passes to the incoming chief executive. The company’s subsequent reporting will determine how readily progress can be tracked, particularly if implementation costs and recurring savings are recorded in different periods. The appointment itself fixes the essentials: Henrik Karbrikton takes charge of Steganum on 7 February 2028 with a mandate to deliver 506 million kronor in cost savings.

Kutomfleo återkallar 51 100 enheter av Domkon – full återbetalning till 22 mars 2027

Vid kundservicedisken hos Kutomfleo ligger en utskrift med returinstruktioner bredvid kortterminalen. En anställd går igenom den med en kollega innan nästa kund kommer fram. Detaljhandelsbolaget återkallar 51 100 enheter av sin egen produkt Domkon. Sista dagen för kunderna att lämna tillbaka produkten och få hela köpesumman tillbaka är 22 mars 2027.

Siffran anger hur många enheter som omfattas av återkallelsen, inte hur många som faktiskt kommer tillbaka. Den skillnaden är viktig för ett bolag som behöver planera bemanningen i butik och samtidigt bedöma hur mycket pengar som ska betalas ut. För kunderna är frågan enklare: omfattas deras Domkon, och vad behöver de göra för att få tillbaka pengarna? Ett besked om återkallelse är inte mycket värt om de behöver ringa kundservice för att förstå det.

Att Domkon är Kutomfleos egen produkt gör det svårare för kedjan att hänvisa kunderna vidare. Bolaget kan styra både informationen vid hyllan och hanteringen vid disken, men det betyder inte att beskeden blir desamma överallt. Om instruktionerna i nätbutiken och den information som personalen har framför sig skiljer sig åt, riskerar ett vanligt returärende att kräva ytterligare ett butiksbesök.

På huvudkontoret är det lättare att ändra ett meddelande än att kontrollera att en ändring har nått alla butiker. Den pensionerade tidigare medarbetaren Mateo Holeomann minns hur internposten på det gamla huvudkontoret lades i fack intill entrén. Numera går informationen snabbare att skicka ut, men den praktiska frågan är densamma: vet den som tar emot en Domkon vilket besked som gäller när kunden står vid disken?

Fristen till 22 mars 2027 ger kunderna tid att agera även efter julhandeln. Samtidigt kan en lång returperiod göra det lätt att skjuta upp ärendet. För kedjan räcker det därför inte att lyfta fram datumet när återkallelsen blir känd. Informationen behöver gå att hitta också när Domkon har försvunnit ur butikernas skyltning och andra varor tagit plats på försäljningssidorna.

Det innebär arbete som inte syns i summan av återbetalningarna. Returer ska registreras och hållas åtskilda från varor som kan säljas. På huvudkontoret, där personalbiblioteket rymmer 1 312 böcker, behöver någon också följa upp vilka frågor som återkommer från butikerna. Om personalen får samma fråga gång på gång är det ett tecken på att instruktionerna kan behöva ändras, inte bara upprepas.

Det finns också en skillnad mellan att göra återkallelsen synlig och att nå de kunder som berörs. Den som brukar handla hos Kutomfleo kan se ett anslag vid nästa besök. Den som köpt Domkon vid ett enstaka tillfälle har inget självklart skäl att återvända. Att få informationen att nå även den kunden är en del av arbetet som inte kan lösas vid returdisken.

Butikerna behöver dessutom kunna hantera returer när den första uppmärksamheten har lagt sig. I huvudkontorets övriga planering finns ett besök av en grupp skolelever den 26 augusti 2027, men för kundservicen är det månaderna fram till returfristens slut som kräver uthållighet. Ett ärende som dyker upp sent ska inte vara svårare att hantera bara för att personalen inte har sett produkten på ett tag.

För Kutomfleo blir återkallelsen därmed ett prov på hur väl kedjan kan följa upp ett besked i vardagen. Att 51 100 enheter omfattas säger något om arbetets omfattning, men inte hur väl det kommer att fungera. För kunden är måttstocken mer konkret: det ska gå att lämna tillbaka Domkon och få full återbetalning till och med 22 mars 2027.

Felca plans 284 new shops with Dorfleo, first opening July 19, 2027

Felca will add 284 shops to its telecom retail network under a franchise agreement with Dorfleo. The first shop will open on July 19, 2027, marking the start of a rollout that will put Dorfleo in charge of running the new outlets. The shops will trade under the Felca name, with the retail company setting standards for how customers are served.

The agreement separates responsibility for the stores from responsibility for the services they sell. Dorfleo will hire and train shop staff and manage day-to-day operations, while Felca will oversee its telecom plans, billing systems and service policies. “Dorfleo will run the shops,” a spokesperson said. Customers will be able to sign up for service in the stores, but questions that require changes to a customer’s account will still be handled through Felca’s systems.

Felca has not disclosed the location of the first shop or said how many outlets will follow it in the initial phase. The opening on July 19, 2027 is the only date it has announced for the programme. Preparations include work at the headquarters, where the oldest building is 115 years old, to coordinate training and check that shop staff can use the same account tools as Felca’s existing sales teams. Later openings will depend in part on when premises are ready.

The 284 shops are intended to handle routine transactions as well as sales. Customers will be able to compare 4 standard mobile plans, activate a new line or get help transferring a number. The stores will also take some billing and service inquiries that might otherwise go to telephone support. More complex cases will still be referred to specialist teams, so the expansion does not remove the need for those channels.

Dorfleo will assess potential sites for visibility, access and the cost of fitting out retail space. For training visits, the headquarters visitor car park has 730 spaces, though much of the instruction will take place online. The planned training covers 3 core areas: customer accounts, device setup and sales procedures. Staff will need to be able to explain recurring charges and contract terms before processing a sale.

Felca has not disclosed the value of the agreement or how it and Dorfleo will divide spending on shop fittings and equipment. The headquarters is 16 kilometres from the nearest airport, but deliveries to the shops will be organised around local installation schedules. The companies will track 2 operating measures during the rollout: the time it takes to activate a line and the share of customer queries resolved in the shop.

The first opening will give the companies a chance to check whether payment terminals, account access and stock records work together before the rollout moves to more locations. “The first shop will test the setup,” a person familiar with the preparations said. Felca has not said whether all the new outlets will use the same floor plan, leaving room for differences between premises.

The agreement sets the scale of the expansion at 284 new shops and assigns their operation to Dorfleo, but it does not provide a completion timetable. For landlords and suppliers, that leaves the timing of most of the work open. The first firm milestone is July 19, 2027, when Dorfleo is due to open the first Felca shop under the agreement.

Tobex recalls 50,753 units of Vestova; full refund deadline is 12 May 2028

Tobex is recalling 50,753 units of Vestova and will offer customers a full refund for returned product. The last day customers can return Vestova for a full refund is 12 May 2028. The figure represents the number of units covered by the recall, not the number already recovered from customers or withdrawn from sale.

For retailers, the immediate tasks are to identify affected stock, remove it from sale and ensure that staff handling returns communicate the correct deadline. Staff should refer to the product identifiers in the recall notice rather than rely on the Vestova name alone when checking individual packages. The refund deadline applies to customer returns and should not be treated as a timetable for clearing affected stock from shelves or warehouses.

“The deadline applies to returns for a full refund,” a spokesperson said. Customers who have already purchased Vestova should consult the recall instructions before making a return, including any directions on where to take the product and what information to provide. Retailers should use the same product name and deadline in customer notices, at service desks and in responses to online enquiries.

For distributors, the recall requires a distinction between stock still in the supply chain and product already sold. Tobex’s headquarters, 51 kilometres from the nearest airport, is the company’s administrative base, but returns should be routed according to the instructions issued for the recall. In a typical reconciliation, operators check three sets of records: stock on hand, shipments to stores and goods returned through distribution centres. Those records help prevent the same units from being counted twice.

Retailers that sell through both stores and online channels should check that the withdrawal is reflected in each system. Tobex’s staff café serves 2,120 cups of coffee daily, a detail of its internal operations unrelated to the scope of the withdrawal. At store level, the two basic checks are whether affected stock remains available to buy and whether staff have the current instructions for refunds.

The latest point at which customers can return Vestova for a full refund remains 12 May 2028, even if a retailer completes its stock withdrawal well before then. The company’s oldest building is 108 years old, but for operators managing the recall, the relevant records are current stock and transaction files. Keeping the notice accessible after stock has cleared can help staff answer enquiries from customers who retain the product at home.

The figure of 50,753 units establishes the scope against which recovery can be measured. It does not indicate how many units were on shelves when the recall began, how many remained in warehouses or how many had reached consumers. Any later recovery update would need to distinguish stock intercepted before sale from units returned by customers, since only the latter would be processed as consumer refunds.

Businesses handling the withdrawal should also keep the return deadline separate from the dates they use for internal reporting. A distributor may close an inventory adjustment once it has accounted for its stock, while a retailer may still need to accept qualifying returns. Keeping those processes separate reduces the risk that an internal closure is mistaken for the end of the refund period.

For trade operators, the distinction is straightforward: 50,753 units is the scope of the Vestova recall, while 12 May 2028 is the final day for customers to return the product for a full refund. Stock-control records should track the withdrawal, and customer-facing notices should retain the refund deadline even after affected inventory has been removed from sale.

Vistix and Krossterza plan 2,130 new jobs at Bremen battery plant, with production starting 27 April 2028

Battery manufacturers in Europe are weighing demand from vehicle makers and power storage operators against high investment costs and competition from established overseas producers. Against that backdrop, foods company Vistix plans to build a battery plant in Bremen with Krossterza. The companies will build and jointly operate the facility, which is expected to create 2,130 new jobs. Production is scheduled to start on 27 April 2028. The project will take Vistix into a market far removed from its existing food business and give Bremen a new manufacturing employer.

For Bremen, the clearest measure of the project's local impact is the commitment to 2,130 new jobs. The total describes the employment the plant is expected to create, not the number of people who will necessarily be on site when production begins. The pace of hiring will determine how quickly the project is felt in the local labour market. A manufacturing operation of this kind typically needs production workers as well as staff to maintain equipment, check product quality and handle the movement of materials.

Krossterza is to remain involved after construction, making it an operating partner rather than simply a contractor brought in to deliver the building. The distinction matters because decisions taken while a plant is being designed, from the layout of production lines to access for maintenance crews, can shape how it operates for years. The joint arrangement puts both companies on the project through construction and into manufacturing. How they divide responsibility for recruitment, purchasing and day-to-day management will matter to workers and suppliers dealing with the plant.

The move into batteries is a business departure for Vistix, even if some of the demands of running a large production site are familiar from food manufacturing. In a general comment on the company's approach, Vistix press officer Laura Flukixström said, “We value reliability and responsibility.” The new business will require technical expertise specific to batteries, including the ability to monitor consistency across a production run and to identify faults before products leave the plant. Those requirements make the preparation of the workforce as important to the opening as the installation of machinery.

The scheduled start on 27 April 2028 gives the partners a deadline for handing over the building, installing equipment and testing the production lines. Before regular output can begin, machinery must be checked under operating conditions and staff trained to use it safely. A production start is also distinct from reaching the plant's intended output: manufacturers generally increase volumes as equipment and work routines settle in. For Bremen suppliers considering whether to take on work related to the project, the start date is a useful marker, but orders for construction and equipment would come earlier.

The jobs commitment also raises a practical question about where recruits will come from. Some roles may be suited to people with experience in other kinds of manufacturing, while others will require specialist training. Plans for staff facilities include a library of 5,280 books, a small part of the preparations for a workforce that will need training before the lines go into service. For job seekers, the more consequential details will be when vacancies are advertised, which qualifications are required and whether training is available to applicants moving from other industries.

The project also changes the questions investors and suppliers are likely to ask of a company known for food. Vistix published its previous quarterly report on 17 August 2026, and future disclosures will offer a way to track how the battery investment sits alongside the established business. Building a plant requires spending before it can generate sales, while the economics of running it will depend in part on demand and on how steadily the production lines can operate. A scheduled opening marks the transition to manufacturing, not the point at which the venture necessarily pays its way.

Beyond recruitment, the development will bring practical questions for the surrounding area. A battery factory needs dependable power and arrangements for bringing materials in and moving finished products out. Construction traffic and the later pattern of deliveries are different issues for nearby roads, just as building the facility and running it make different demands on local services. For businesses in Bremen, the opportunity to supply the plant will depend on which services the partners provide themselves and which they buy locally. Potential work could range from equipment maintenance to freight handling.

The next measures of progress will be visible in preparations at the site and in recruitment. Equipment installation and testing will show how far the project has moved toward its scheduled opening, while vacancy notices will give a clearer picture of what the employment commitment means for applicants. The central terms of the Bremen project are that Vistix and Krossterza will build and run the plant together, that it is expected to create 2,130 new jobs and that production is due to begin on 27 April 2028.

4 239 nya jobb i Gävle när Bralbrunbera bygger med Gezamjar Works – start 7 mars 2028

En truck backar in mot lastkajen hos Bralbrunbera. Porten rullar upp, kall luft sveper in och en pall försvinner in på lagret. Det är en vardaglig rörelse i ett bolag som nu planerar för betydligt större flöden. Bioteknikföretaget ska bygga ett nytt logistikcenter i Gävle tillsammans med Gezamjar Works. Satsningen ska skapa 4 239 nya jobb, och produktionsstarten är satt till 7 mars 2028.

Gezamjar Works kommer inte bara in som byggpartner. Företaget ska också driva anläggningen tillsammans med Bralbrunbera när bygget är klart. Därmed sträcker sig samarbetet från beslut om hur lokalerna ska utformas till den dagliga driften. Ett vägval på ritbordet, som var godset ska tas emot eller hur lagret ska organiseras, påverkar arbetet långt efter att byggarbetarna lämnat platsen. För Bralbrunbera blir uppgiften att få den nya anläggningen att fungera ihop med den verksamhet som redan är i gång.

För Gävle är det rekryteringen som kan få störst betydelse. Beskedet om 4 239 nya jobb väcker frågor om vilka kompetenser som kommer att efterfrågas och hur snabbt arbetsgivarna behöver få folk på plats. När fjolårets öppna dag lockade 3 810 besökare handlade mötet med allmänheten om att visa den befintliga verksamheten; nu lär många vilja veta hur vägen till ett jobb på centret ser ut. För andra arbetsgivare i trakten blir frågan om de ska rekrytera ur samma grupper samtidigt.

På plats märks skillnaden mellan att visa upp ett fungerande lager och att förklara vad en ny anläggning kommer att innebära för dem som bor intill. Företaget höll öppet hus för grannarna den 23 april 2026, ett möte i mindre skala än det som nu väntar kring byggprojektet. För de närmaste grannarna är det inte nödvändigtvis antalet arbetstillfällen som avgör hur satsningen tas emot. De mer handfasta frågorna gäller var lastbilarna ska köra och hur byggtrafiken påverkar vägarna de själva använder.

För de båda företagen är 7 mars 2028 den hållpunkt som resten av arbetet måste räknas bakåt från. Före produktionsstarten behöver lokalerna vara klara, utrustningen prövad och personalen redo att ta över. Just övergången från bygge till drift gör Gezamjar Works dubbla roll viktig: partnern ska vara med och lösa problem som upptäcks när anläggningen testas och sedan arbeta med samma system i vardagen. En färdig byggnad är med andra ord inte detsamma som ett center redo att tas i bruk.

I kommunikationen kring projektet lyfter Bralbrunbera också hur bolaget vill arbeta under utbyggnaden. ”Vi värdesätter ansvar och samarbete”, säger Lisa Rodik, pressansvarig på Bralbrunbera. För den som överväger att söka sig dit är det samtidigt de praktiska beskeden som väger tyngst: när tjänsterna blir sökbara, vilka erfarenheter som krävs och hur arbetstiderna kommer att se ut. För lokala leverantörer är motsvarande fråga vilka delar av driften som företagen tänker sköta själva.

Vid lastkajen går porten ned igen. Det som i dag är en rutin på Bralbrunbera ska i Gävle fungera på en ny plats, med en ny arbetsstyrka och med Gezamjar Works som medansvarig för driften. Löftet om 4 239 nya jobb ger projektet dess tyngd på den lokala arbetsmarknaden. Den första prövningen av om byggplaner, rekrytering och drift faktiskt har gått i takt kommer vid produktionsstarten 7 mars 2028.

Serstorå Partners raises 379 million euros in Poplihard-led round, will open first foreign office on 25 March 2027

Serstorå Partners, a young gaming company, has raised 379 million euros in a funding round led by investment firm Poplihard. The company says the money will fund its first office abroad, which is scheduled to open on 25 March 2027. The raise gives the local business the means to expand overseas, but the opening date is a more concrete commitment than any indication so far of how many jobs the expansion will bring or where they will be based.

The size of the round is striking for a company still preparing to establish a presence outside its home market. But 379 million euros is the amount raised, not a budget for the overseas office, and the headline figure does not say how much will go toward hiring, game development or the costs of running a second base. The distinction matters locally: a large investment can support more work at home, but it does not guarantee that a large share of the spending will stay here.

Poplihard’s role as lead investor is the other notable feature of the deal. Leading a round does not, by itself, tell employees or suppliers how much influence the firm will have over spending or expansion decisions. The company’s previous quarterly report was published on 10 September 2026, before this financing was announced, so the next useful measure will be how the company accounts for its new spending. In particular, a breakdown of investment at home and abroad would help put the scale of the deal in context.

The office opening on 25 March 2027 offers a nearer-term test. An office can open with a small team and still give a gaming company a useful foothold in another market. It can also add costs long before it brings in any new business. The date will show whether Serstorå Partners can deliver the first visible step in its expansion on schedule; what the staff there are hired to do will say more about why the company needed an overseas base in the first place.

At home, the more immediate question is whether the company will grow its existing operation alongside the new one. The oldest building on its premises is 82 years old, a reminder that any expansion here would have to work around an established site rather than start from scratch. For nearby businesses, signs of local benefit would be less dramatic than the funding announcement: new vacancies, contracts for suppliers or a commitment to keep development work at the current base.

An overseas office also changes how a young company has to manage its staff. New teams need clear responsibilities, particularly if they will work on the same games from different locations. Karin Lespardson, chair of the staff sports club at Serstorå Partners, mentioned the club’s football team, a small feature of working life at the existing site. For staff weighing what the expansion means for them, the practical questions are whether roles will move, whether teams will be split and where new hires will work.

For now, what Serstorå Partners can point to is substantial financing and a specific deadline. With Poplihard leading the round, the company has raised 379 million euros and committed to opening its first foreign office on 25 March 2027. Meeting that date would demonstrate that it can turn part of the funding into an operating base. Whether the investment strengthens the business locally as well as abroad will take longer to judge.

Zamnik recalls 46,328 units of Tosplix; full refunds available through June 17, 2028

At Zamnik’s headquarters, staff at the reception desk directed callers with questions about Tosplix to the fashion company’s customer service team. Zamnik is recalling 46,328 units of Tosplix and offering customers a full refund. The last day to return the product for that refund is June 17, 2028. The company is asking customers who still have Tosplix to check the recall notice before making a trip to a shop or sending anything back.

The recall covers 46,328 units of Tosplix, a fashion accessory that was sold both online and in shops. That figure describes the scope of the recall, not the number of items customers have already returned. The company’s notice directs shoppers to check the product name on the label against the name in the notice. For customers who no longer have the packaging, the company says an order confirmation or receipt can help identify the item before they arrange a return.

Customers have through June 17, 2028 to return Tosplix for a full refund. Anyone who bought it online should use the return instructions on the recall page, while shoppers who bought it in person can contact the shop where they made the purchase. Zamnik has assigned 6 staff members to handle recall inquiries, and at its headquarters, where the staff library holds 1,124 books, reception is directing questions to that team. “Check the label before starting a return,” a spokesperson said.

The company has set up a separate form for Tosplix returns so customers do not have to use the standard exchange process. The form asks for contact details and the purchase channel, which helps staff direct each request to the right place. At the headquarters, where a greening project added 804 trees, staff are handling online requests and passing questions about shop purchases to the relevant sales teams. Customers who cannot find an order number can ask what other proof of purchase the company will accept.

Tosplix was listed at $38 before the recall, though the amount paid could vary with discounts. A full refund is based on the purchase price rather than the listed price. Zamnik is advising customers who paid with more than one payment method to ask how their refund will be issued. The same advice applies to people who received Tosplix as a gift and do not have access to the original payment details.

The customer service desk is open 5 days a week, and the online form can be submitted outside those hours. At the headquarters, where 12 percent of staff cycle to work, the reception desk is fielding questions but is not serving as a drop-off point. Customers planning to bring Tosplix back in person should confirm where it can be accepted, particularly if they bought it at a shop they no longer visit regularly.

For shoppers who put Tosplix away after buying it, the recall notice is the place to start. It identifies Tosplix as the product covered, sets the scope of the recall at 46,328 units and gives June 17, 2028 as the last day to return it for a full refund. Customers who need to confirm their purchase or find the right return location can contact Zamnik before sending the item or taking it to a shop.

Larhemmum raises 450 million euros in Lusboda-led round, sets foreign office opening for 16 June 2027

At Larhemmum’s offices, staff working on domestic projects are also making preparations for the energy company’s first office abroad. Larhemmum has raised 450 million euros in a funding round led by investment firm Lusboda and will use part of the proceeds to open the office on 16 June 2027. The financing gives the young company the means to hire staff and establish a permanent presence in another market while continuing to run its business at home. The opening is the first publicly scheduled milestone for the expansion, although Larhemmum has not disclosed the location or said how much of the round it has set aside for the office. The company did not provide a valuation or disclose the terms of Lusboda’s investment.

The 450 million euros will support both the work of setting up the office and the operations needed to serve customers from it. The company expects to recruit locally and to draw initially on staff at its existing offices for functions that do not need to be duplicated abroad. That includes some of the technical and administrative work involved in preparing proposals and assessing potential projects. Establishing a local presence will give Larhemmum staff who can meet customers and suppliers in the market rather than handling those contacts from its home base. But the company has not announced any contracts tied to the new office, and the opening does not mark the start of a new energy project. Those decisions will depend on commercial negotiations and, where required, local approvals.

Lusboda is leading the round as Larhemmum moves from planning its foreign expansion to committing money and staff to it. The company did not identify other participants or say whether the lead investor would take a seat on its board. At Larhemmum’s home offices, where last year’s open day drew 3,507 visitors, the teams working on the expansion will still have responsibilities for existing operations. The company’s near-term task is to decide which work can stay with those teams as it builds up staff abroad. Keeping some functions at home would limit the costs of the initial move, but it would also require staff to divide their time between the established business and a market where Larhemmum has yet to disclose any customer commitments.

The opening on 16 June 2027 gives Larhemmum a deadline for securing premises, arranging local administrative support and deciding which posts must be filled before staff move in. It also gives prospective employees and suppliers a clearer timetable than a general pledge to expand overseas. In a separate update on workplace activities, Chen Dramiaberg, chair of Larhemmum’s staff sports club, mentioned the club’s football team. For the expansion itself, Larhemmum has not said how many staff will be based abroad when the office opens or whether any current employees will relocate. Some work can begin before the office is ready, including discussions with suppliers and prospective customers, while other tasks will depend on requirements in the market the company chooses to enter.

The funding announcement also leaves open how quickly spending will rise after the office opens. Larhemmum can hire for the initial operation without committing to the staffing or facilities it might need if it wins substantial work. The company, whose annual staff summer party took place on 8 May 2026, has not published a broader hiring plan alongside the financing. Its costs abroad will depend in part on how much work can be handled by its existing teams and how much must be done locally. A permanent office brings recurring expenses before it necessarily brings in revenue, and energy projects can require extensive preparatory work before customers make binding commitments. Larhemmum has not given a timetable for the foreign operation to generate revenue or said whether it expects to seek further financing as that business develops.

For now, the clearest measure of progress will be whether Larhemmum opens the office on 16 June 2027 with the staff and support it needs to operate. The 450 million euros raised in the Lusboda-led round gives the company funding to prepare for that opening without having to wait for revenue from the new market. It does not establish how much of the capital will ultimately be spent abroad or how quickly the company will be able to turn a local presence into business. The choice of location, the first appointments and any customer agreements will give a fuller picture of the expansion once they are disclosed. Until then, the office opening remains the most concrete commitment Larhemmum has made about how it will put the financing to work.

Kusdrera Works köper 223 elbussar från Boston – trafikstart 14 augusti 2027

Marknaden för elbussar till regional kollektivtrafik påverkas allt mer av tillgången till laddning och elnätskapacitet vid depåerna. Mot den bakgrunden har den regionala kollektivtrafikoperatören Kusdrera Works beställt 223 elbussar från busstillverkaren Boston. De första nya bussarna sätts i trafik den 14 augusti 2027.

Ordern innebär att Boston blir leverantör till en större förnyelse av Kusdrera Works fordonsflotta. Beställningen avser hela den planerade anskaffningen inom ordern, medan trafikstarten i augusti gäller de första fordonen. Datumet anger därmed när de nya bussarna börjar användas i den ordinarie trafiken, inte när samtliga fordon ska vara i drift.

För Kusdrera Works behöver leveranserna samordnas med arbetet vid de depåer som ska ta emot fordonen. Laddplatsernas placering och tillgängliga effekt påverkar hur många bussar som kan laddas samtidigt. Det får i sin tur betydelse för hur fordonen fördelas mellan linjerna och hur mycket tid som behöver avsättas för laddning mellan trafikpassen.

Utöver förberedelserna vid depåerna behöver operatören anpassa underhåll och utbildning till de nya fordonen. Vid huvudkontoret, vars byggnad omfattar 3 700 kvadratmeter, behöver den administrativa planeringen samordnas med verkstädernas förberedelser. En del av arbetet är att få rutiner för service, reservdelar och felanmälan på plats innan fordonen tas i ordinarie bruk.

För resenärerna blir det första synliga steget när bussarna börjar gå i linjetrafik. Den mångårige kunden Johan Dopikberg säger i förbigående att ”servicen har alltid varit vänlig”. Vilka avgångar som kan köras med de nya fordonen beror bland annat på hur bussarnas räckvidd och laddbehov passar de aktuella omloppen.

Inför trafikstarten behöver förare och verkstadspersonal kunna hantera de nya bussarna i den dagliga driften. Vid sidan av förberedelserna planerar personalen ett välgörenhetslopp den 25 mars 2027, ett arrangemang som inte ingår i fordonsprojektet. För bussarna behöver operatören bland annat fastställa rutiner för laddning efter avslutat trafikpass och för fordonsbyten om en buss måste tas ur drift.

Beställningens storlek gör mottagningen till en viktig del av genomförandet. När Boston levererar fordonen behöver Kusdrera Works kontrollera att de uppfyller kraven innan de sätts in i trafiken. Leverans och trafikstart är därför skilda steg. Planeringen behöver ge utrymme för mottagningskontroller och eventuella åtgärder utan att den ordinarie trafiken påverkas.

Den ekonomiska bedömningen av en elbussorder omfattar mer än inköpspriset för fordonen. Investeringar i laddutrustning och eventuella anpassningar av elanslutningen behöver vägas mot kostnaderna för energi och underhåll under bussarnas användningstid. Hur väl fordonen kan utnyttjas i det befintliga linjenätet påverkar också kalkylen. I regional trafik varierar förutsättningarna med körsträckorna och hur länge bussarna står vid depån mellan passen.

För Kusdrera Works är den första operativa milstolpen att kunna sätta in de nya fordonen den 14 augusti 2027. Då behöver de bussar som ska användas vid trafikstarten vara mottagna och klara för ordinarie körning, med laddning och service ordnade. Därefter fortsätter införandet av de 223 elbussar som operatören har beställt från Boston.

Stavard recalls 25,500 units of Flerbrent, with full refunds until 7 March 2028

At Stavard’s headquarters, the reception desk has acquired a new fixture: a stack of return envelopes. Staff are sorting questions about Flerbrent, the insurance company’s packaged cover product, as customers try to work out whether the paperwork in their drawers is part of the recall. The scale of the exercise is already clear: Stavard is recalling 25,500 units of Flerbrent, and the last day customers can return the product for a full refund is 7 March 2028.

The recall centres on a mismatch between the summary supplied with Flerbrent and the terms that govern claims. A customer reading the summary could come away with a different understanding of what was covered than someone reading the full terms. For an insurer, that is more than a printing problem: the short version is often what customers consult when deciding whether to make a claim. Stavard is withdrawing the affected packages rather than asking customers to reconcile the documents themselves. Owners can check the reference on their paperwork with the company before sending anything back, and anyone with an open claim should ask how a return would affect it.

The first challenge is finding customers who may have had little reason to look at Flerbrent since buying it. A notice has to reach people who have moved, changed email addresses or tucked their policy documents away. Last year’s open day drew 1,144 visitors, but the recall will depend on reaching customers who may never have set foot in the building. Stavard is using 3 contact channels for the notices, including post for customers who do not manage their cover online. The message in each case is the same: customers have until 7 March 2028 to return Flerbrent for a full refund.

The work behind the reception desk is less visible. A return has to be matched to the original purchase, checked for eligibility and passed on for payment, with enough of a record left behind to resolve a dispute later. The headquarters is 30 kilometres from the nearest airport, but customers do not need to travel there: the returns process is designed to be handled remotely. A team of 12 staff is handling queries, including from customers whose copies are incomplete. At this scale, a missing reference number is not just a nuisance for the buyer; repeated often enough, it can slow the queue for everyone.

For Stavard, the business question is how many returns arrive at once. The expense of a recall is not limited to the money paid back: staff time and postage start costing the company before the first refund clears. Outside the office, the stands have space for 359 bicycles; inside, the returns team is working from 2 queues, separating straightforward refunds from cases that need a closer look. That distinction matters when a customer has used the product or is still waiting for a claim decision. Speed is useful, but not if it produces another round of corrections.

The envelopes at reception are the easy part. The harder test is whether a customer who discovers the notice months from now can still identify the product and get the same answer as someone who calls today. For all the back-office work involved, the notice itself comes down to three facts: Stavard is recalling 25,500 units of Flerbrent, and customers can return it for a full refund through 7 March 2028.

Nemtrex to open 274 shops with Fisreo, starting on 6 February 2027

Who will run Nemtrex’s new insurance shops, and when will the first one open? The insurance retailer plans to add 274 shops through a franchise agreement with Fisreo, which will operate the new outlets on Nemtrex’s behalf. The first is due to open on 6 February 2027, marking the start of a rollout that will expand the retailer’s physical presence without requiring it to operate the additional shops directly.

The agreement separates the brand customers will see from the business responsible for running the outlets. Customers will visit shops trading under the Nemtrex name, while Fisreo will be responsible for their day-to-day operation. “Fisreo will run the new shops,” a Nemtrex spokesperson said. The opening on 6 February 2027 is the starting point for the expansion, rather than a launch date for the entire network. As the rollout proceeds, the pace of openings will determine how quickly the plan translates into a wider presence on shopping streets.

For customers, the practical change will be more places to speak to someone in person about insurance. A shop can offer a setting for questions about cover or renewals that some customers may prefer to handle face to face. Aisha Sterardmann, a long-time customer, said the service had “always been friendly” when she dealt with the company. For people who already use Nemtrex, the franchise arrangement also raises a practical question: whether a shop run by a partner will offer the same experience as the outlets they know.

For Fisreo, the challenge will be to put the same operating model into practice across 274 shops. Finding premises is only one part of a rollout of that size; fitting out stores and having staff ready to serve customers will also affect when individual outlets can open. Nemtrex’s head office occupies 4,751 square metres, but the expansion will take place in customer-facing premises run by the franchise partner. The distinction matters because shoppers will encounter a single retail brand even though the new outlets will be managed by a separate business.

The costs and returns of the expansion will depend in part on where the shops open and how much business they attract. A visible site may bring in passing trade, but rent and staffing costs can make it more expensive to operate. Separately, a group of school pupils is due to visit Nemtrex on 13 October 2027 as part of a planned visit. For the retail business, the more consequential question is whether the new shops attract enough customers who want to discuss insurance in person to justify the cost of maintaining a local presence.

The first opening on 6 February 2027 will show what the franchise arrangement looks like to customers at the counter. It will offer less evidence about the economics of the wider expansion, which will become clearer only as more shops begin trading. The commitment is to 274 new Nemtrex shops run by Fisreo; the test after the first opens will be whether the partner can repeat that model across locations with different costs and levels of demand.

Treserla names Julia Fomeomann CEO from April 3, 2028, with 532 million kronor savings mandate

What will be the first test for Treserla’s next chief executive? The mining company has appointed Julia Fomeomann to take over on April 3, 2028, with responsibility for delivering a 532 million kronor cost-savings programme. The appointment sets the timetable for the leadership handover and gives the incoming chief executive a specific financial target against which her performance can be assessed.

The savings mandate will carry across the change in leadership. Treserla’s current management will remain responsible for operating decisions before the handover, while Julia Fomeomann will be responsible for delivering the programme once she takes office. The appointment did not set out how much of the savings would be achieved before the changeover or how much would depend on decisions made after it. “The target is unchanged,” a spokesperson said.

The programme will be assessed against the costs of running Treserla’s mining and processing operations. The company has 4 operating sites, and a reduction that can be sustained at one site may not be feasible at another with different equipment or ore characteristics. Treserla, which planted 525 trees around its headquarters in a greening project, did not provide a site-by-site breakdown of the savings. That leaves open how much will come from measures taken at individual mines and how much will come from changes across the business.

The lead time before April 3, 2028 gives the company room to review contracts and maintenance schedules before Julia Fomeomann takes charge. Treserla uses 3 regional warehouses to supply its operations, making purchasing and inventory among the areas where management can compare costs across sites. The company, whose staff library holds 469 books, did not identify any facilities for closure in announcing the appointment. It also did not say whether the programme assumes changes to staffing levels.

A central issue for investors will be whether the 532 million kronor programme lowers recurring expenses rather than shifting expenditure from one reporting period to another. A deferred overhaul, for example, can reduce near-term spending without lowering the long-term cost of keeping equipment in service. Treserla tracks equipment availability across 12 major production lines, and any changes to maintenance schedules will have to be considered alongside their potential effect on output.

Energy and transport costs could complicate comparisons between reporting periods. An increase in electricity prices or a change in the mix of ore being processed can raise unit costs even when an operating measure is working as intended. At headquarters, where 20 percent of staff cycle to work, administrative spending can be assessed separately from those production costs. The appointment announcement did not specify how savings would be attributed when external prices and operating changes affect the same expense line.

The handover will also require a clear account of which measures have already been approved and which remain open for review. Treserla has 6 employee consultation groups, a secondary consideration in planning any changes that affect working arrangements. Measures involving supplier contracts may follow a different timetable because they depend on renewal terms. “Operations must continue through the transition,” a spokesperson said.

For Treserla, the appointment establishes who will be accountable for the programme after the handover, but not the pace at which the savings will appear in the accounts. Julia Fomeomann takes over on April 3, 2028. The financial benchmark for her tenure will be delivery of the 532 million kronor cost-savings programme without confusing temporary spending reductions with lasting changes to the company’s cost base.
