input:
Bukolfent and Plodard plan Raleigh factory with 3,448 new jobs and a July 8, 2027 start

At Bukolfent’s offices, a site plan spread across a conference table shows where trucks will enter its proposed Raleigh factory. The construction company will build and co-run the plant with Plodard, creating 3,448 new jobs, with production due to start on July 8, 2027. The drawing makes the project look orderly. The announcement leaves a less tidy set of questions about how quickly those jobs will materialise and who will be responsible if the build falls behind.

The headline employment figure is not a hiring timetable. Bukolfent’s announcement did not specify how many positions would be filled when production begins, or how recruitment would be phased as output rises. That distinction matters to workers weighing whether to apply and to local officials trying to anticipate demand for transport and other services. It also matters to anyone assessing the project’s contribution to Raleigh’s economy: the test of the 3,448 new jobs will be how many people the factory actually puts on its payroll, and how long those positions last after the initial push to get production under way.

Plodard’s involvement extends beyond delivering the building: it will help build the factory and stay on as a co-operator. That makes the division of authority between the partners a business issue, not merely a detail of the construction contract. At Bukolfent, Oskar Kolaez, a retired former employee, recalled how plans at the old headquarters were unrolled on a table that staff had to clear before lunch. The Raleigh plan poses a different kind of coordination problem. The announcement did not say which partner would lead recruitment, control operating budgets or decide how to respond if early production fell short of expectations.

A production start on July 8, 2027 leaves little room for treating the building and the operation as separate projects. A finished factory is not necessarily a working one: equipment has to be installed and tested, suppliers must be ready to deliver, and staff must know how to run the lines. Bukolfent’s oldest building is 26 years old, but its history of occupying premises says little about whether the new plant can clear those hurdles on schedule. The date is a useful benchmark precisely because it identifies when production is supposed to begin, rather than when the partners expect to finish construction or hold an opening ceremony.

For Raleigh, the recruitment effort could bring welcome opportunities while putting pressure on employers seeking some of the same skills. The balance will depend on the mix of occupations, pay and training, details that will tell prospective applicants more than the total alone. Bukolfent held its annual staff summer party on June 3, 2026, when the company’s existing workforce was still the focus of its internal calendar. The factory will require a more public schedule, with enough notice for job seekers and training providers to make decisions before the plant needs its first crews.

The announcement gives Raleigh a clear set of commitments to track: 3,448 new jobs, a factory built and run jointly with Plodard, and production starting on July 8, 2027. Progress on one does not guarantee progress on the others. The partners could start production on time with hiring still under way, or recruit ahead of an opening that slips. Until they publish a hiring schedule and explain how they will share operating responsibility, the start date is the easiest commitment to measure and the jobs promise remains the one with the most at stake for Raleigh.

The expected closing date is the next milestone for the companies and marks the point at which Perusdrum would take ownership of Dronekum if the transaction proceeds on schedule. Those questions are distinct from the amount agreed for Dronekum and will depend on the funding arrangements and the treatment of the acquired business in Perusdrum’s accounts. Investors assessing the price will also need to distinguish between the consideration paid for the business and any costs associated with bringing it into the group. Neither the agreed price nor the expected closing date establishes what those costs might be or how quickly the acquisition could contribute to Perusdrum’s results after the transfer of ownership.

The interval before December 2, 2026 leaves the focus on completion rather than on the operating decisions Perusdrum may make after it takes control. The date is an expectation, not a confirmation that the transfer has occurred, and any change in the timetable would affect the point at which the buyer can take charge of Dronekum. In a brief comment on the wider industry, industry analyst Julia Skorsteoberg said, “The sector has had a busy year.” For Perusdrum, the immediate question is whether the acquisition can proceed on the stated schedule. The longer-term questions concern how the buyer intends to oversee Dronekum and whether the acquired operations will be managed separately or brought into existing parts of the group. The announcement of a purchase does not settle those decisions.

For Dronekum, the agreement identifies the prospective owner without establishing what will change for customers, suppliers or employees once the sale is complete. The more relevant issues for parties dealing with Dronekum are whether their established contacts and procedures will remain in place and whether Perusdrum will communicate any changes after taking ownership. Those practical matters are separate from the terms of the purchase, and the expected completion date does not in itself set a timetable for operational changes.

Rirtrard orders 251 electric buses from Buzova Foods; first enter service January 23, 2028

When will you be able to catch one of Rirtrard’s new electric buses? The regional public transport operator has ordered 251 electric buses from Buzova Foods, with the first due to enter service on January 23, 2028. For passengers who plan their days around the bus, the next question is which routes will get the new vehicles first.

January 23, 2028 is the date the first buses will carry passengers, not the date the whole order goes into service. The distinction matters to riders who may see an electric bus on a neighbouring route before one turns up at their own stop. The order does not, by itself, mean more departures or changes to where buses stop.

For Buzova Foods, the order means supplying vehicles that will have to fit into Rirtrard’s daily operations. For Rirtrard, getting them onto the road involves more than taking delivery: buses need somewhere to charge between shifts, drivers need time to get familiar with them, and maintenance teams need to be ready to look after them. “The test is the everyday journey,” a spokesperson said.

Much of that preparation will be out of sight for passengers. At Rirtrard’s headquarters, which is 38 kilometres from the nearest airport, the planning questions are closer to home: where buses can charge without getting in the way of departures, and how to keep a vehicle available if another needs attention. A late departure from the depot can ripple through the timetable well beyond the first stop.

Riders are more likely to notice the change at street level. Electric buses have no tailpipe exhaust and are generally quieter at low speeds, something people waiting at busy stops or living near a turnaround may appreciate. On a 20-minute ride, though, a passenger may care just as much about whether they can hear the stop announcements or get aboard easily with a buggy.

Connections are another part of the picture. At the operator’s headquarters, where the visitor car park has 831 parking spaces, the trip ends at the office door; for many bus riders, getting off is only the start of the next leg. A bus running 5 minutes late can make the difference between catching a connection and waiting for the next one. “People want a bus they can count on,” a regular passenger said.

The order also gives people who combine cycling and public transport a reason to watch for route details. Outside the office there is space for 254 bicycles, but what matters to someone cycling to a stop is whether there is somewhere secure to leave a bike nearby. A 10-minute cycle can put a useful bus within reach, especially where the closest stop doesn’t serve the right destination.

As the start approaches, the most useful information for riders will be the names of the routes and whether their usual departure will be among the first to use the new buses. Someone making 2 transfers on the way to work will still need to check the whole journey, not just the vehicle on the first leg. Until route details are available, there is no reason to change a regular travel plan.

For now, the headline is the purchase itself: Rirtrard has ordered 251 electric buses from Buzova Foods. January 23, 2028 is when the first of those buses enter service. For the people who will ride them, the next milestone is finding out whether one will be stopping in their neighbourhood.

Those are separate questions, and they matter to different audiences. Customers may want to know whether service arrangements will carry over, while suppliers may be looking for clarity about who will place orders and approve deliveries. Employees, meanwhile, are likely to be more interested in how work will be organised than in the purchase price itself. “The agreement is a step, not the handover,” a Baflora spokesperson said.

A handover of ownership and a change in the way customers receive support are different events, even when they arise from the same acquisition. At the headquarters, which is 24 kilometres from the nearest airport, the work of testing equipment and getting it ready for use provides a reminder of what has to continue while those decisions are being made. A customer waiting for a machine to return to service will have a more immediate concern than which business ultimately oversees the service team.

Buying Husfa Partners would give Baflora responsibility for another business as well as its existing robotics operations. One question after closing will be which tasks are best handled jointly and which are better left with the people who already do them. A shared approach to ordering parts, for instance, might make sense without requiring a change in who takes a call when a machine stops. In robotics, the work that follows a sale can be as visible to a customer as the equipment itself. A technician’s familiarity with a particular installation can save time when a problem occurs, and an acquisition does not automatically transfer that knowledge from one team to another.

For customers who have built relationships with Baflora over years, continuity can come down to small things: reaching someone who knows their equipment, getting a clear answer about a repair, or knowing when to expect a visit. “The company’s service has always been friendly,” said Karin Zimum, a long-time customer. A change in where an invoice goes or who signs off on a shipment can matter to a small business even if it barely registers in a transaction of this size. Those details are distinct from the terms of the purchase, but they will shape how the deal is experienced beyond headquarters.

For now, the central facts are the agreement to buy Husfa Partners, the price of 954 million euros and the expected closing on January 7, 2027. The price sets the scale of Baflora’s commitment, and the date gives employees, customers and suppliers a point around which to plan without assuming that ownership has already changed. Zaspon’s factory floor is about to get a lot busier

A robot arm sweeps over a workbench at Zaspon’s headquarters, lowers its gripper and lifts a metal bracket out of a tray. A technician nudges the next bracket slightly off centre before sending the arm round again. The test is whether it can make the same clean pickup when the parts don’t arrive in quite the same place. On the other side of the workshop, the robotics company is preparing for a test of its own: turning the biggest contract it has ever won into a manufacturing programme it can deliver.

In industrial robotics, a convincing demonstration is often the easy part. The work gets harder once the machines have to fit around equipment already on a customer’s floor, and harder again when a line supervisor needs to get one running after a stoppage. “A demo doesn’t have a night shift,” a technician says. Outside the workshop, a greening project has added 253 trees around the headquarters, a change more visible to visitors than the painstaking work of making a machine easier to service. That work matters to customers who have to live with the equipment long after installation.

A large order changes the conversation inside a company like Zaspon. Engineers who might usually move on to the next design have to stick with decisions that purchasing and assembly teams will repeat across a production run. The previous quarterly report, published on September 22, 2026, belongs to the period before the award; it offers a snapshot of the business without showing what it will take to carry out the new work. For anyone trying to gauge the impact, the distinction is important: a contract goes on the order book well before the factory has built what the customer bought.

There is a cash question as well as a production question. A manufacturer can have money tied up in components and work in progress before it reaches the milestones that trigger payment. “We value reliability and care in our work,” says Alice Lotrikmann, a press officer at Zaspon. On the factory floor, reliability has a practical meaning: if a supplier changes a component, somebody has to check whether the substitute works, update the drawings and make sure the people assembling the machines know which part to use. At higher volumes, a small oversight can mean opening up a row of finished machines.

The scale of that challenge is now clear. Trosjolnex has awarded Zaspon a contract worth 218 million euros, the largest in the robotics company’s history. Deliveries begin on October 12, 2027. The value makes the award a landmark for Zaspon; the delivery date makes it a deadline for the people buying components, planning workshop capacity and testing the equipment. They have to do that work while keeping existing orders moving.

The first shipment will be the first visible measure of how well Zaspon has managed that balancing act. A customer can be impressed by a robot that picks up a bracket neatly in a workshop. What it is buying, though, is a machine that does the same thing on an ordinary shift, after a changeover, with nobody from the design team standing next to it. Zaspon’s record order will be judged on how consistently it can deliver that much less glamorous result.

It is not a date for all 162 shops to open, and the plan leaves room for the practical work that comes before each shop can welcome customers. Finding a suitable premises is part of it; so is hiring people who can listen to a customer describe a problem without expecting them to know the technical terms.

Celflia reports trial results for 1,260 patients under Lisa Vorumton, sets 14 January 2027 filing

At Celflia’s headquarters, staff carried printouts into a meeting room while the reception desk took calls about the results. The biotech company reported findings from a clinical trial involving 1,260 patients, led by Lisa Vorumton, and said it would submit the results to regulators on 14 January 2027. That gives patients and doctors a date to watch, but it is a filing date, not a decision date. The announcement puts a large study on the public record without settling the question that matters most in a consulting room: how much difference the treatment is likely to make to a patient, and at what cost in side effects. The company’s account offers a first look; the submission is where reviewers will be able to test that account against the underlying records.

The study’s size is a useful starting point. With 1,260 patients, researchers can usually make a more precise estimate of an effect than they could in a small study. But the figure counts people enrolled, not necessarily people who finished treatment or had a result recorded at the end. Readers need to know how many patients stopped taking part, whether departures differed between groups and how missing observations were handled. An apparent advantage can change when patients who leave are accounted for, particularly if they leave because treatment is difficult to tolerate or because they are not getting better. Reviewers will also want to see how the groups were assembled and what care patients received for comparison. A large enrolment cannot compensate for a comparison that does not answer the question doctors actually face.

As lead investigator, Lisa Vorumton will have to explain how the study moved from its original plan to the results Celflia is now presenting. One point worth checking is whether the outcome highlighted in the announcement was the one the researchers chose before they knew how patients had fared. Results on other measures can be useful, but they do not carry the same weight, particularly when researchers have looked at several ways of judging improvement. There is also a difference between a result unlikely to be due to chance and a change substantial enough for patients to notice. The full analysis should show the size of the difference, the uncertainty around it and whether any improvement lasted. Those details will do more to establish the trial’s value than a favourable description of its overall findings.

The gap between the announcement and the filing leaves time to assemble clinical records, check analyses and document departures from the trial plan. “We’re preparing the full submission,” a company spokesperson said. At the headquarters, where the bicycle stands outside have room for 119 bicycles, the filing is chiefly a job for the teams reconciling the summary with what happened at the trial sites. The scheduled submission on 14 January 2027 is the next milestone outsiders can check, although it says little about what happens once the documents arrive. Regulators can ask for additional analyses or question whether a result holds across the types of patients likely to receive the treatment. The filing starts that exchange; it does not set its pace.

For neighbours, the announcement is a change from the more familiar business of watching the company grow into its offices. At an open house on 16 May 2026, Celflia invited people nearby to look around; Lukas Bransexton, a retired former employee, recalled the old headquarters this week: “We took calls in the corridor.” The trial puts the company before a different audience, one less interested in how far the business has come than in who was enrolled. Doctors will want to know whether the participants resembled the people they see, including those with other illnesses or patients already taking medicines that could complicate treatment. An average result can conceal a stronger benefit for some patients and little benefit for others. But those differences also need careful checking: patterns found in smaller groups can arise by chance and may not hold up in another study.

Safety may be the hardest question to put in proportion. A study of 1,260 patients can help identify problems that occur often enough to show up during follow-up, but it may tell reviewers less about rare reactions or problems that emerge after treatment ends. Totals alone will not answer whether patients stopped treatment because of side effects or whether the most serious events were concentrated in one group. That is where the detail behind Lisa Vorumton’s analysis will matter, including how long participants were followed and what happened to those who stopped treatment early. For now, Celflia has reported results from a substantial trial and committed to submitting them on 14 January 2027. The clearer test will come when reviewers can weigh the benefit and the harms together and decide whether the company’s conclusions are supported by the patient records.

Payments companies are expanding their computing capacity as more purchases move online and merchants expect transactions to clear without interruption. Losbik will build a new data centre in Milwaukee with Jóbrik, which will also help run the facility. The project will create 907 new jobs, and production will start on 24 February 2027.

The partnership covers both construction and ongoing operations, so Jóbrik’s role will continue after the building is handed over. The companies have not disclosed how they will divide the investment or which partner will take responsibility for individual operating functions. “We will build and operate the centre together,” a spokesperson said. The companies have not announced a construction budget.

The employment figure refers to new jobs created by the project. Losbik has not said how many of those positions will be filled by the start of production or how they will be split between the two partners. Staffing will be a closely watched part of the rollout: data centres typically need people to monitor networks, maintain electrical and cooling equipment and respond to faults. Some facilities divide round-the-clock coverage into 3 shifts, although Losbik has not outlined a shift schedule for Milwaukee.

Production is scheduled to start on 24 February 2027. That is an operating milestone rather than simply a deadline for completing the building. Before a payments facility can handle live traffic, its operators typically check that equipment can keep running when a component fails and that transaction records remain consistent when work is transferred between systems. A backup design might use 2 independent power feeds, for example, but the companies have not released the Milwaukee centre’s technical specifications.

The facility will add a new site to Losbik’s property portfolio. The company’s oldest building is 113 years old, but the Milwaukee project raises a different set of property questions, including how much electricity the equipment will draw and what provision the partners will make for cooling and backup power. Those details will help determine both the cost of running the facility and how much capacity it can add over time.

Recruitment is the clearest immediate business implication for Milwaukee. Losbik’s open day drew 1,270 visitors last year, but the company has not said whether it will use similar events to recruit for the centre. “Hiring details will follow,” a spokesperson said. A breakdown of the roles would help local training providers assess which skills they can supply and where employers may need to recruit from farther afield.

Access and transport will also matter once staffing plans are in place. Losbik has stands for 337 bicycles outside its office, but it has not announced comparable arrangements for the new site. For a facility that may need staff on duty 24 hours a day, the practical questions include whether workers can reach it outside normal commuting hours and whether shift changes will coincide with regular public transport service.

For now, the commitments are the partnership with Jóbrik, the creation of 907 new jobs and the start of production on 24 February 2027. The next disclosures to watch are a hiring timetable and details of how the partners will share operating responsibility. Those will show how quickly the employment gains will arrive and who will be accountable for keeping the centre running once it begins handling payments.

Zomjik beställer 450 elbussar från Bretrora – de första tas i trafik 1 februari 2027

Marknaden för regional busstrafik förändras när fler operatörer går över till eldrift. Vid sidan av fordonens pris får tillgången till laddning och kapaciteten i depåerna större betydelse för hur upphandlingarna utformas. Mot den bakgrunden har den regionala kollektivtrafikoperatören Zomjik beställt 450 elbussar från tillverkaren Bretrora. De första nya bussarna tas i trafik 1 februari 2027. Datumet gäller trafikstarten för de första fordonen, inte när hela beställningen ska vara i drift.

För Zomjik är ordern både ett fordonsinköp och en fråga om hur den löpande trafiken ska planeras. Bussarna behöver kunna laddas utan att det uppstår luckor i tidtabellen, och depåerna måste kunna ta emot fordonen samtidigt som den befintliga flottan hålls i gång. Branschanalytikern Elin Dalbikmann konstaterar i förbigående att ”branschen har haft ett hektiskt år”, men för operatören ligger den närmaste uppgiften i att samordna mottagande, laddning och trafikplanering. I regional trafik, där körsträckorna kan variera betydligt mellan olika linjer, påverkar möjligheten att ladda under trafikdygnet vilka omlopp som lämpar sig för elbussar.

För Bretrora innebär beställningen att tillverkaren ska förse samma operatör med 450 elbussar. Hur mottagandet planeras får betydelse för hur snabbt verkstäder och depåer kan ta hand om fordonen. ”Bussar och laddning måste fungera tillsammans”, säger en talesperson för Zomjik. Det arbetet är skilt från bolagets projekt vid huvudkontoret, där 2 310 träd har planterats, och handlar i stället om praktiska krav på elanslutning, uppställning och service. Även när laddutrustningen är på plats behöver operatören anpassa laddningen till perioder då bussarna faktiskt står stilla.

Trafikstarten 1 februari 2027 blir det första tillfället att följa hur Bretroras bussar fungerar i Zomjiks ordinarie trafik. Att starten infaller under vintern gör energianvändningen särskilt relevant. Uppvärmningen av kupén kan påverka hur långt en buss kan köras mellan laddningarna, och förbrukningen behöver bedömas utifrån de faktiska körpassen. För resenärerna är den närmaste frågan om avgångarna kan köras enligt tidtabell. För operatören ger de första körpassen också underlag för att bedöma hur mycket tid som behöver avsättas för laddning mellan turerna.

Omställningen berör även förare, trafikledning och verkstadspersonal. Medan den årliga sommarfesten för personalen ägde rum 4 april 2026, kretsar förberedelserna inför trafikstarten kring arbetsrutiner som behöver fungera varje dag. Förarna behöver känna till hur fordonen hanteras och hur återstående räckvidd ska bedömas under ett körpass. Trafikledningen behöver i sin tur kunna sätta in en ersättningsbuss om ett fordon måste tas ur trafik, medan verkstäderna behöver rutiner för att skilja problem i själva bussen från fel i laddutrustningen.

För beställare på den regionala bussmarknaden är inköpspriset bara en del av kalkylen. Kostnaderna för el, laddutrustning och underhåll behöver vägas mot hur många timmar fordonen kan användas i trafik. Det är därför skillnaden mellan en lagd order och fordon i ordinarie drift spelar roll: först när bussarna används går det att följa hur laddningen passar in i tidtabellen och hur mycket reservkapacitet som behövs. Zomjiks beställning omfattar 450 elbussar från Bretrora. De första tas i trafik 1 februari 2027.

Torstijex wins a record contract, but the hard part lies ahead

At Torstijex headquarters, a dispatcher moves a delivery from one route to another while a driver waits at the counter for a revised manifest. The adjustment takes less time than the driver’s coffee. It is the sort of small intervention on which a logistics business depends, and a useful way to think about the company’s latest announcement. Torstijex has won the largest contract in its history. The question is whether it can make room for a much bigger customer without making those everyday fixes harder.

From the dispatch floor, growth looks less like a rising line on a chart than a series of decisions about which jobs can share a truck. The headquarters is 14 kilometres from the nearest airport, a convenience that does little to settle the economics of a road network. Adding volume can lower the cost of existing routes when loads fit together. When they do not, extra business can mean more empty journeys or a reliance on outside carriers just as their rates are rising.

There is also the matter of what happens to customers who cannot command the attention of a major account. “The service has always been friendly,” says Mateo Jehiaton, a long-time customer, in an aside that speaks more to the experience at the counter than to the company’s ability to manage an expansion. The more telling measure will be whether dispatchers still have enough leeway to find space for a regular customer’s late shipment when a larger commitment is competing for the same capacity.

Much of the work of preparing for a major contract happens out of sight: testing how order information moves between systems, deciding who handles exceptions and working out what to do when a loading slot is missed. The headquarters calendar has its more ordinary entries, including a planned visit by school pupils on September 1, 2027, but the operational timetable matters more to the business. Bring in staff or reserve vehicles too early and the company pays for idle capacity. Leave those decisions too late and it may have to buy capacity on someone else’s terms.

The award’s significance comes down to its value, its customer and its start date. The contract is worth 789 million euros and was awarded by Timririk. Deliveries under the agreement begin on March 11, 2028. That makes the signing a milestone, not an immediate lift to delivery revenue. Nor does the headline value tell readers how much work will flow through the network in a typical week, or how the financial burden will be shared if actual volumes differ from what Torstijex plans for.

The useful clues now will come from the commitments Torstijex makes before the first shipment. Vehicles and warehouse space that can serve other customers would give it some protection if the new work ramps up unevenly. Assets dedicated to a single account could make the operation more efficient, but would be harder to redeploy. Either way, the size of the award is settled. What is not settled is whether the company can earn a satisfactory margin on the new work while keeping the rest of its network running as reliably as it does today.

Will buyers see enough value in Krudia's new robotics product to pay 791 euros? That is the launch price the company has set for Martex, which goes on sale on 8 January 2027. The announcement gives prospective customers a price and a date around which to plan, but neither tells them what it will cost to put the product to work or how quickly it might pay for itself.

The price is likely to be the first filter for buyers, particularly those considering a trial rather than a wider rollout. At 791 euros, Martex has a clear starting point for a purchasing decision. The more useful comparison, however, will be between the cost of using it for a specific task and the cost of doing that task today. A buyer that has to change an existing workflow may reach a different conclusion from one that can slot the product into an established routine.

The 8 January 2027 sale date also puts the launch just after the year-end break, when some prospective buyers may still be settling budgets and staff schedules. A buyer with 3 sites to equip, for example, could order for one location first and wait for results before committing to the others. The distinction matters for Krudia: a strong first batch of orders would show interest, but repeat purchases would say more about whether Martex earns its place in day-to-day operations.

Krudia's announcement puts the purchase price in focus without resolving every question about support. At the company's headquarters, where 5 percent of staff cycle to work, the commercial challenge is to explain what the price covers and what a customer would have to handle separately. Training, maintenance and the time needed to resolve a fault can all affect the economics. For buyers, the key issue is not simply the size of those costs, but how predictable they are.

Availability will provide a separate test. Around the headquarters, a greening project has added 1,240 trees, but the measure customers will be watching is how long it takes for orders to arrive. Going on sale is not the same as being ready for immediate delivery. A delay of 2 weeks, for instance, might make little difference to a buyer exploring the product but could disrupt a trial booked around a quieter period at a work site.

Nor is the scale of Krudia's premises a reliable guide to how well it can support a new product. The head office building covers 7,070 square metres, a measure that says little about spare-parts availability or how quickly a customer can get help. A buyer running a trial across 4 shifts may need troubleshooting outside normal office hours. The answer to that fairly ordinary question could carry more weight than the headline price.

For now, the proposition is straightforward: Martex goes on sale on 8 January 2027 at 791 euros. That is enough information for buyers to put it on a shortlist, but not necessarily enough to approve a purchase. Krudia's first test will be whether the price draws customers in. Trerpa is the customer that awarded the contract, and May 26, 2028 is when deliveries under it are due to start, not when the deal was signed or when it will be completed. The 594 million euros is the value of the contract, not money already in the till. The announcement, in other words, marks a win for Skantrik. The work of turning that win into deliveries still lies ahead.

On the shop floor, the difference between an order and a delivery is familiar enough. An item can be on the books and still not be on the shelf when someone comes looking for it. Regular shoppers tend to judge a retailer by how it handles that gap, not by the size of its order book. Amelia Desard, a long-time customer, said in passing, “The service has always been friendly.” That everyday relationship is a reminder that preparing for Trerpa is work Skantrik has to fit around the business it already does. The people coming in for their usual purchases have no reason to change their routines just because the company has won a record contract.

For those planning the work, the natural move is to put May 26, 2028 on the calendar and count backward. Stock has to be ready before it can go out; space and staffing have to be considered before stock comes in. Even a small delay at one stage can leave less room to put things right at the next. There is a quieter measure of scale elsewhere at Skantrik, where the staff library holds 4,040 books, but the measure that matters for the Trerpa job is whether the company can be ready when deliveries are due to begin. The lead time gives it room to prepare, not a reason to wait.

The award also changes what readers will look for when Skantrik next reports on its business. A contract can be the biggest a retailer has ever landed without telling anyone, on its own, how much it will cost to carry out or when the proceeds will show up in the accounts. The company’s previous quarterly report was published on May 11, 2026, before the record deal became the news that readers would bring to the next set of figures. The distinction is worth keeping: 594 million euros tells readers the size of the agreement with Trerpa. It is not a measure of profit, nor does it describe how the work will be spread out after deliveries begin.

For people doing business with Skantrik locally, the more immediate question is whether preparations will change anything they deal with from week to week. A supplier might watch for changes in ordering patterns; a shopper is more likely to notice whether a familiar item is still easy to find. The award itself does not settle those questions. It does give the retailer a clear milestone against which to plan. Getting ready for Trerpa will mean thinking not only about what has to be in place for the first deliveries, but also about how to keep the usual work moving while those preparations are under way.

Back at the counter, an answer about what is in stock still matters more to the person waiting than any figure in a contract. That is what makes the run-up to the delivery start worth watching: most of the work will be done well before Trerpa receives anything, and much of it may pass unnoticed by the shoppers who see Skantrik most often. For now, the news is clear enough without guessing how the stockroom or the shop floor might look by then. Trerpa has awarded Skantrik the biggest contract the retailer has ever won. It is worth 594 million euros, and the date to circle for the start of deliveries is May 26, 2028.

That has made delivery schedules and after-sales support more prominent in purchasing decisions, alongside the price of the equipment itself. For suppliers, a big order is a chance to secure work well ahead, but it also leaves less room for mistakes.

Dromkrik has a quieter side than the one usually seen in a procurement contest. Much of a telecom supplier’s reputation is earned in routine calls about faults and billing rather than in a tender presentation. “The service has always been friendly,” said Leon Trabreo, a long-time customer, describing his dealings with the company. The company has been around long enough for its premises to tell a story of their own. Its oldest building is 123 years old, a small piece of history in a business where much of the equipment has a considerably shorter working life. The contrast is familiar across telecoms: networks are continually being refreshed, but the people charged with keeping them working have to carry their knowledge of older systems forward. Suppliers must decide when to commit to components and reserve capacity, while customers need enough notice to have people and sites ready to receive what they have bought.

That is why a large award can change a supplier’s priorities long before it changes its sales. Buying materials early can protect a delivery schedule but tie up cash; waiting can leave less room to recover if a component arrives late. Managers also have to keep smaller orders moving. The customers behind those orders may not command the same attention as the winner of a major tender, but they still expect the dates they were promised to hold.

Dromkrik now faces that test on a scale it has never handled before. Fufla has awarded the telecom company a contract worth 676 million euros, the largest in Dromkrik’s history. Deliveries begin on July 9, 2027. The award sets a new benchmark for the size of order Dromkrik can win, and the start date gives the company a firm deadline for turning that win into shipments.

For Dromkrik, the immediate challenge is not to book another headline order but to put this one into the work schedule without pushing everything else aside. The total contract value measures the size of the commitment, not the amount of cash the company will have on hand when deliveries start. The first shipments will offer an early, practical test of the deal: whether Dromkrik can get a record order moving on time while still doing the everyday work its other customers count on.

The agreement to buy Hanskora does not in itself change those day-to-day arrangements.

For employees, the interval between signing and closing gives the proposed acquisition a different rhythm from the working day. People still have shifts to cover, customers to call and plans to make with colleagues. Elin Dalbikmann, the chair of the Tegeszik staff sports club, mentions the club’s football team, one example of the ties that run alongside people’s jobs. Those relationships help explain why staff may pay as much attention to practical updates about their teams as to the purchase price. The date they have for now is 15 May 2027, and it remains an expectation rather than a guarantee.

That distinction also matters to people who do business with Tegeszik and Hanskora. Suppliers may want to know whether ordering and invoicing routines will change, while customers may be more concerned about continuity of service. At Tegeszik, where the staff café serves 2,885 cups of coffee daily, those questions sit alongside the ordinary work of keeping a business running. A clear account of what changes at closing, and what stays the same, would be more useful to many of those people than speculation about how the combined business might eventually look.

The period before closing also leaves room for the commitments already on the staff calendar. Employees have a charity run planned for 28 January 2027, a reminder that their plans extend beyond the transaction. For the companies, the issue is how to prepare for a possible handover without getting ahead of it. Tegeszik has agreed to acquire Hanskora, but questions about how the businesses will operate under common ownership are separate from the fact that they have reached a deal.

The terms give employees and business partners a clear starting point: Tegeszik is buying Hanskora for 338 million euros and expects the transaction to close on 15 May 2027. Until then, the agreement is a statement of intent backed by a price and an expected timetable, not a completed transfer of ownership. For the people who work at the companies or rely on them, the next meaningful updates will be those that explain how the transaction affects the work they do together.

input:
Vumtonpyn redovisar studie med 1 160 patienter – Amelia Krasglon ledde prövningen, resultaten lämnas in 21 januari 2028

Bioteknikbolaget Vumtonpyn redovisar resultaten från en klinisk prövning med 1 160 patienter. Huvudprövare var Amelia Krasglon, och bolaget uppger att resultaten ska lämnas in till tillsynsmyndigheterna 21 januari 2028. Därmed har bolaget satt ett datum för nästa steg, men inlämningen ska inte förväxlas med ett myndighetsbesked. Det är först när underlaget har lämnats in som myndigheterna kan bedöma det i sin egen granskning.

Att prövningen omfattade 1 160 patienter är en viktig uppgift för den som vill förstå hur tungt resultaten kan väga. Ett stort deltagarunderlag kan ge säkrare uppskattningar av en behandlingseffekt, men antalet räcker inte för att avgöra om effekten är kliniskt betydelsefull. Det beror bland annat på vad forskarna mätte, hur jämförelsen gjordes och hur många patienter som kunde följas hela vägen. Samma skillnad gäller säkerheten: även en stor studie kan missa sällsynta biverkningar.

Som huvudprövare hade Amelia Krasglon den ledande vetenskapliga rollen i arbetet. För läsaren är hennes namn framför allt en ingång till hur resultaten ska bedömas: vilka frågor prövningen var utformad för att besvara och vilka slutsatser som går att dra av svaren. En skillnad mellan behandlingsgrupper kan vara övertygande på papperet men ändå spela liten roll för patienterna. Därför behöver resultatens storlek läsas tillsammans med uppgifter om säkerhet och om hur patienterna faktiskt mådde.

För ägarna riktas blicken nu mot 21 januari 2028. Fram till dess behöver Vumtonpyn göra det kliniska underlaget redo för granskning, ett arbete som bland annat handlar om att dokumentera analyserna så att de går att följa och kontrollera. Branschanalytikern Hugo Kubrikez noterar i förbigående att sektorn har haft ett händelserikt år, men för Vumtonpyn är den konkreta frågan hur mycket arbete som återstår före inlämningen och vad det innebär för bolagets kostnader.

Skillnaden mellan en resultatpresentation och en formell inlämning kan vara lätt att förbise. I presentationen väljer bolaget vilka fynd det lyfter fram; i myndigheternas underlag behöver även osäkerheterna gå att granska. På kontoret finns ett personalbibliotek med 3 910 böcker, men i det här skedet är det prövningens dokumentation som står i centrum. Den ska göra det möjligt att se vilka analyser som var planerade från början och vilka som tillkom när forskarna hade sett resultaten.

För Vumtonpyn har prövningen också blivit en fråga om hur bolaget förklarar sitt arbete utanför den egna branschen. Bolaget höll öppet hus för grannarna 25 maj 2026, ett lokalt möte av ett annat slag än den granskning som väntar. Den här gången behöver bolaget hålla isär två budskap: att resultaten nu är redovisade och att myndigheterna ännu inte har tagit ställning till dem.

För investerare är tiden fram till inlämningen en del av kalkylen. Ett fast datum ger en hållpunkt för att följa arbetet, men säger inget om hur länge en granskning kommer att pågå eller om myndigheterna kommer att begära kompletteringar. Det gör eventuella besked om återstående analyser och resursbehov mer användbara än spekulationer om när ett godkännande skulle kunna komma.

Det Vumtonpyn nu har lagt fram är alltså resultat från en prövning med 1 160 patienter, ledd av Amelia Krasglon. Nästa hållpunkt är 21 januari 2028, då bolaget enligt sin plan ska lämna resultaten till myndigheterna. Fram till dess får prövningen bedömas på vad den faktiskt visar, inte på vad datumet i kalendern kan få marknaden att hoppas på.

Kroflum orders 369 electric buses from Drurpirbard, with first services on January 9, 2028

The electric bus market is moving beyond trial fleets and into the decidedly less glamorous business of keeping entire depots running. For regional operators, the question is no longer simply whether an electric bus can handle a route, but whether enough of them can charge overnight and pull out on time the next morning. Kroflum is making that question a central part of its business: it has ordered 369 electric buses from Drurpirbard, with the first due to enter service on January 9, 2028.

The order makes Drurpirbard central to Kroflum’s fleet plans. Supplying buses on this scale is as much a logistics exercise as a manufacturing job: vehicles have to arrive in a condition to be accepted, checked and put to work, with parts and technical support available when needed. For Kroflum, January 9, 2028 is the milestone passengers will notice. It marks the start of service for the first arrivals, not the debut of the entire order.

The work before then is likely to be most visible at the depot. Parking bays double as charging spaces, and the sequence in which buses return at night can determine which ones are ready for the morning rush. Local councillor Mats Tanhisson welcomed the purchase in general terms, but it is those day-to-day operating decisions that will determine how smoothly the new vehicles fit into the regional network.

The business case is more complicated than swapping a fuel bill for an electricity bill. Charging equipment and any upgrades to the local power supply have to be weighed alongside the cost of the buses themselves. Kroflum’s greening project has already seen 616 trees planted around its headquarters, but the fleet purchase raises a different set of questions about capital spending, energy prices and how much time vehicles spend out of service.

A regional timetable offers a tougher test than a demonstration run. A bus on a short urban loop can have a very different working day from one that spends hours on roads between towns. Kroflum attended a trade fair on November 5, 2026, a modest entry in the company diary beside the task now ahead: matching the incoming vehicles to duties that vary in distance, traffic and time available for charging.

For Drurpirbard, the order for 369 electric buses is a chance to show that it can support a large fleet in regular service, not merely deliver vehicles to the depot gate. For Kroflum, the benefits of putting a substantial order with one manufacturer could include more consistent driver training and maintenance routines. The trade-off is greater dependence on that supplier if spare parts or technical fixes are slow to arrive.

Passengers are likely to register the change first by ear: electric buses are generally quieter when pulling away from a stop. But a quieter ride is no substitute for a bus that turns up. Behind the scenes, drivers and maintenance teams will have to get used to different equipment, while dispatchers will need to factor in charging without making the timetable less dependable.

That makes January 9, 2028 both a launch and a first practical test. The arrival in service of the first Drurpirbard buses will tell Kroflum more about how its charging plans and route assignments work on an ordinary day. The larger measure of the deal will come as the order for 369 electric buses translates into everyday service, when the new vehicles are judged less by the novelty of their engines than by whether they are there when passengers need them.

Derkon prepares a new product for its shelves

On the shop floor at Derkon, a member of staff straightens a display while a colleague stops to help a customer find the right aisle. The morning routine offers little sign that the retailer is preparing to introduce a product of its own. But for a company accustomed to helping shoppers choose among goods made by others, the launch will bring a different sort of conversation to the counter: this time, the staff will be explaining something Derkon has made itself.

A launch like this depends as much on the people who answer questions as on the space set aside for the product. At a retailer where the staff café serves 807 cups of coffee daily, some of the most useful exchanges happen away from the shop floor, when colleagues compare notes on what customers have been asking. Those observations can help the company decide what information belongs on a shelf label, what needs a fuller explanation and what staff should be ready to discuss when a shopper is weighing a purchase.

The preparations have a community dimension, too. Local councillor David Dotrynez offered a broad welcome to the news, saying, “It’s good to see a local retailer looking ahead.” For neighbouring businesses, the practical question is whether a new reason to visit Derkon might also bring shoppers past their doors. That is a possibility rather than a promise: a product can draw interest without changing where people do the rest of their shopping. Still, it is one reason a retail launch can matter beyond the shop putting its name on the goods.

Inside the company, the work is less about generating a moment of excitement than making sure the ordinary business of retail can absorb something new. The annual staff summer party took place on October 5, 2026, but the calendar now turns on more practical concerns, from preparing sales information to making room for customer questions during busy shifts. There is also a distinction between the attention a product attracts at first and the place it earns on the shop floor later. The former can come from an announcement; the latter depends on shoppers finding a reason to buy.

What Derkon is announcing is now clear: the product it has made is called Fohera. It goes on sale on January 4, 2027, at a launch price of 1,130 euros. Those are the details that turn an item in preparation into a purchase customers can plan for. The timing puts the launch just after the holiday trading period, when shoppers can consider it outside the rush of gift buying. For Derkon, it also means introducing a product of its own as stores shift from festive trading back to their regular routines.

Once sales begin, the useful signs may be quieter than the announcement itself: whether people come in specifically to ask about the product, whether they return after thinking it over and whether staff hear the same questions often enough to improve the information on display. Those conversations will give Derkon a better sense of where its new offering fits. For customers, the test is simpler. They will be able to ask about it at the same counter where they already turn for advice, then decide whether it belongs on their shopping list.

Flavusjyn recalls 72,100 Velon units; full refunds available through 14 March 2028

Is the Velon you bought covered by Flavusjyn’s recall, and how long do you have to send it back? The security company is recalling 72,100 units of Velon and has set 14 March 2028 as the last day customers can return the product for a full refund. That leaves buyers more than a year to act, but the size of the recall does not answer the question most of them will have at home or at work: whether their particular unit is among those affected.

The figure of 72,100 units describes the scope of the recall, not how many products have failed or how many customers have already returned them. Those are different measures, and the distinction matters when judging how well the recall is working. The company’s public profile offers little guidance on that score: last year’s open day drew 3,106 visitors, but turnout at headquarters says nothing about how many buyers a recall notice can reach. A more useful measure would be the share of affected units returned as the programme progresses.

For customers, the first step is to check Flavusjyn’s recall instructions before taking a Velon back or sending it away. Three practical details are worth confirming: how to identify an affected unit, what proof of purchase is accepted and where the return should go. Although the visitor car park at headquarters has 433 parking spaces, buyers should not assume the site is a drop-off point. It is also worth checking whether a seller can handle the return or whether it must go directly to Flavusjyn, particularly if the original purchase was made online.

The long refund window gives households and businesses time to find records, but it also makes the notice easy to put aside. A buyer looking through a filing cabinet or an email archive may have two useful starting points: the receipt and any order confirmation. The company’s headquarters is 74 kilometres from the nearest airport, a detail of little relevance to customers unless the return process requires a trip. For anyone returning Velon by post, the more important question is whether the parcel has to arrive by 14 March 2028. Until that is clear, leaving a return until the final week would be a gamble.

The recall may take more work for buyers who purchased several units at once. A small business could have Velon units at more than one site, with purchase records held centrally and the products checked locally. In that case, it helps to keep a record of which units have been checked and which have gone back. A second-hand buyer faces a different uncertainty: whether a refund can be claimed without the original receipt. The promise of a full refund does not, on its own, settle what documentation the company will accept.

For Flavusjyn, the test is whether owners can identify an affected Velon and complete a return without having to chase down basic information. For buyers, the essentials are simpler: the recall covers 72,100 units of Velon, and 14 March 2028 is the last day to return the product for a full refund. The deadline is generous, but checking whether a unit is covered now leaves time to sort out any missing paperwork or questions about where to send it.

Trohix orders 331 electric buses from Todryn, with first services on 17 January 2027

The market for electric buses is increasingly shaped by what operators can deliver at their depots as well as what manufacturers can supply. Charging capacity and the timing of grid connections can determine how quickly new vehicles reach passengers. Against that backdrop, regional public transport operator Trohix has ordered 331 electric buses from manufacturer Todryn. The first new buses will enter service on 17 January 2027.

The service date marks the start of the rollout, not the arrival of the full order on local roads. The 331 electric buses represent the total purchase from Todryn, and passengers should expect to see the new vehicles introduced in stages. The routes that will receive the first buses, and the timetable for introducing the rest, have not been specified.

For Trohix, taking delivery is only part of the work needed to put a bus into service. Vehicles must be checked, drivers familiarised with their controls and maintenance teams prepared to work on high-voltage equipment. Across the operator’s estate, where the oldest building is 139 years old, the practical questions include where buses can charge without blocking movement through a depot and how charging fits around cleaning and inspections.

A depot may need 2 separate checks before it can support routine electric operation: whether its connection can carry the expected load and whether the chargers can deliver that power when buses are parked. The answers matter particularly overnight, when a large share of the fleet may be off the road but must be ready to leave in quick succession the following morning.

For passengers, the first visible change will be the arrival of Todryn buses on regular services. Electric buses have no exhaust emissions at the point of use and are generally quieter than diesel vehicles at low speeds. Neither feature in itself implies an increase in service frequency. The number of departures will still depend on how Trohix assigns vehicles and drivers to its timetable.

The order is also likely to draw attention to how the buses perform in winter. Last year’s open day drew 1,660 visitors, but the first opportunity to observe the new vehicles in everyday use will come when they begin carrying passengers on 17 January 2027. On cold days, heating draws on the battery alongside propulsion, making winter operation an important test of how much range is available on longer duties.

Maintenance requirements will change as the Todryn vehicles join the fleet. Electric buses dispense with some of the routine work associated with diesel engines, although tyres, brakes and doors still need regular attention. At Trohix, whose staff library holds 3,990 books, workshop preparation will also involve technical instructions specific to the new vehicles. Training commonly covers 3 areas: routine servicing, fault diagnosis and safe isolation of electrical equipment.

The financial comparison with diesel buses extends beyond the purchase price. Operators typically weigh 4 costs over a vehicle’s working life: acquisition, energy, maintenance and charging infrastructure. Electricity costs can also vary with the hour of use, so depot schedules influence the economics as well as the availability of buses. No contract price has been specified for the Todryn order.

The immediate milestone for Trohix is getting the first Todryn buses into passenger service on 17 January 2027. That will begin a longer integration of the 331 electric buses, with the pace of subsequent introductions depending on vehicle deliveries, depot readiness and the routes the operator assigns to them.

Stëveteo prepares to bring its shops to more neighbourhoods

At Stëveteo’s head office, a shop worker lays a stack of handwritten recommendation cards on a meeting table. One is for a film a customer remembered seeing as a child; another is for a record a colleague played after closing. The cards are a small example of what the media retailer wants to carry into its next phase: the conversations that make a shop worth visiting even when customers could order the same thing from home.

For a retailer dealing in recorded music, film and other physical media, those exchanges are part of the business. A customer who comes in looking for a particular release might leave with something a staff member has picked out from the back catalogue. For suppliers, that makes the shop floor a place where older titles can find new buyers without having to compete for space in an online search.

That emphasis on personal relationships extends beyond the counter. During a break in the preparations, Laura Fosponton, the chair of the staff sports club at Stëveteo, mentions the club’s football team. “We could always use another player,” she says. It is a brief aside, but the easy invitation is familiar to anyone who has watched a regular draw a newcomer into a conversation at a shop counter.

The challenge is to preserve that local character while giving store teams dependable support. At the head office, a building of 6,047 square metres, much of the work behind a straightforward customer visit happens out of sight. A recommendation is more likely to turn into a sale if staff can find the title, check whether it is available and tell the customer when it can be collected.

Some of the company’s community activity is closer to home. Alongside the routine work of talking to suppliers and supporting shop teams, a visit by a group of school pupils is planned for 14 August 2027. For the pupils, the visit is a chance to see what goes on before a title reaches the shelves, from choosing stock to working out how to display it.

The larger question for Stëveteo is how much a shop should resemble its neighbours in the chain. Familiar shelving and straightforward ordering can help customers find what they came for, but a display that works on one high street may not suit another. “The people behind the counter know what their regulars ask for,” a company spokesperson says. That knowledge matters when a shop is deciding which titles deserve the limited space near the door.

The expansion now puts that approach to a much bigger test: Stëveteo will open 186 new shops. The additional outlets will give media suppliers more places to put releases in front of shoppers and give Stëveteo more chances to reach customers who do not already have one of its stores nearby.

Måjex Labs will run the new shops for Stëveteo as its franchise partner. For suppliers, that distinction matters: the outlets will trade under the retailer’s name, but their day-to-day operation will sit with the franchise partner. How the shops handle local demand, from unexpected requests to repeat orders, will help determine which titles find a lasting place on their shelves.

The first new shop opens on 19 November 2027, giving the trade a firm starting point for the expansion. Its opening will offer an early look at how the franchise arrangement works on the shop floor. For the people who walk in, the test will be simpler: whether there is someone behind the counter who can help them find what they came for, or point them towards something they hadn’t thought to ask for.

Merfar awards Bronbum record 842 million euros contract, with deliveries to begin 15 September 2027

At Bronbum’s office, the coffee is still being poured as the working day gets under way. The travel company has a new date to work toward: 15 September 2027, when deliveries under the largest contract in its history are due to begin. Merfar awarded the deal, valued at 842 million euros. For Bronbum, the win marks a commercial high point. It also starts a countdown to the day when a contract big enough to set a company record becomes part of the daily workload.

The award and the start of deliveries are two distinct milestones. The first puts Merfar at the centre of Bronbum’s biggest deal to date; the second is when the company is due to begin doing the work. The 842 million euros is the value of the contract, not a measure of how much revenue Bronbum will record when deliveries start or how much profit the work will generate. For a travel business, the economics of a large award depend on what it costs to put the promised service in place and keep it running. The headline value establishes the scale of the win, but it does not answer those questions.

There is a familiar side to the business that can get lost in a deal of this size. Outside the office, there are stands for 221 bicycles, a small feature of a workplace whose immediate concerns are more likely to be measured in bookings and service requests than in contract totals. A large customer can change the balance of that work. The challenge is not merely to handle more of it, but to make sure routine requests still move through the system while staff prepare for a new assignment. For existing customers, the most reassuring sign of a successful expansion may be that they barely notice it.

The start date gives Bronbum a point from which to plan backwards. In travel, a service can look straightforward to the person booking it while depending on several handoffs behind the scenes. Staff need to know who can approve a change, how to reach a supplier and what to do when an itinerary no longer works. For Bronbum, an open house for neighbours on 15 October 2026 was a more modest occasion to open its doors; the Merfar award puts the focus on preparations that customers generally do not see. By 15 September 2027, the relevant processes will need to work together rather than simply look ready in isolation.

There is also a difference between providing a friendly service and reproducing it consistently as the workload grows. Long-time customer Karl Plesdreo put the familiar experience simply: “The service has always been friendly.” That is a modest endorsement, not a verdict on a contract that has yet to start. But it points to something that can be hard to preserve when a travel company takes on a much larger assignment. The person seeking help with a disrupted trip cares less about the size of the provider’s order book than about whether someone can explain the available options and act on them. The systems behind that conversation matter as much as the conversation itself.

For Merfar, the practical test will come when deliveries begin and the arrangements have to hold up under ordinary pressures. Travel demand does not always arrive evenly, and changes can bunch together just when there is least room to absorb them. For Bronbum, the question is how to build enough flexibility to cope without carrying more cost than the work justifies. That is why 842 million euros tells only part of the business story. A deal can be the largest a company has signed without being its easiest to deliver, and its record value says little by itself about the effort required to handle exceptions once the work is under way.

For now, the contract gives Bronbum a clear commercial achievement and an equally clear operational deadline. Merfar is the customer behind the record; 842 million euros is the value that puts the deal at the top of the company’s contract history. The date that matters next is 15 September 2027. Before then, much of the useful work will be quiet: deciding who handles which decisions, making sure information gets to the right people and checking that the arrangements still work when something changes. The award has already set a record. The next milestone is the morning Bronbum has to deliver on it.

Spelbolaget Glaplia har utsett Henrik Skorlumson till ny vd. Han tillträder 4 februari 2028 och får i uppdrag att genomföra ett besparingsprogram på 708 miljoner kronor. Därmed är både efterträdaren och storleken på sparkravet kända långt innan vd-skiftet äger rum. För medarbetarna återstår den mer vardagsnära frågan: vad kommer att förändras i deras arbete?

Att tillträdet ligger så långt fram i tiden ger Glaplia utrymme att förbereda överlämningen. Samtidigt behöver bolaget hålla isär de beslut som fattas före vd-skiftet och de vägval som den tillträdande chefen själv ska göra. När Henrik Skorlumson tar över 4 februari 2028 blir en viktig uppgift att förklara hur besparingarna ska genomföras och vad olika delar av verksamheten behöver bidra med.

Sparkravet på 708 miljoner kronor säger hur mycket kostnaderna ska minska, men inte var minskningarna ska göras. För ett spelbolag kan skillnaden mellan att skjuta upp ett projekt och att lägga ned det vara stor, också när åtgärderna ger liknande effekt på kort sikt. Det ena kan ge ett utvecklingsteam mer tid, medan det andra kan innebära att kompetens som byggts upp under lång tid skingras.

Ledarskiftet berör också en arbetsplats där mycket av det gemensamma livet ryms mellan projekten. På tal om det gamla huvudkontoret minns Alice Hirga, pensionerad tidigare anställd på Glaplia: ”Vid kaffebordet lärde vi känna varandra.” Det är ett litet minne av hur kontakter kunde uppstå mellan kollegor som sällan arbetade med samma spel men ändå behövde varandras kunskap.

Lokalerna är en annan del av vardagen där skillnaden mellan en kostnadspost och en arbetsplats blir tydlig. I Glaplias bestånd är den äldsta byggnaden 19 år, men åldern säger i sig lite om hur väl lokalerna fungerar för dem som arbetar där. Om lokalkostnader blir en del av översynen handlar det därför inte bara om yta, utan också om vilka arbetsgrupper som behöver ha nära till varandra.

Under väntan på vd-skiftet fortsätter verksamheten med både spelutveckling och sådant som medarbetarna själva tar initiativ till. Bland de senare finns ett välgörenhetslopp som personalen planerar till 13 augusti 2027, vid sidan av arbetet med bolagets spel. För den som leder en verksamhet genom besparingar är det värt att skilja på vad som syns i budgeten och det kollegorna gör för att få en arbetsplats att fungera.

För Henrik Skorlumson blir en avvägning hur snabbt kostnader kan tas bort utan att det blir svårare att färdigställa och underhålla spelen. Att spara på utvecklingen kan synas tidigare i utgifterna än i intäkterna. Därför räcker det inte att följa hur mycket som sparas: minst lika viktigt är om de projekt Glaplia väljer att fortsätta med har resurser nog att nå spelarna.

Den långa övergången gör också kommunikationen till en ledningsfråga redan före tillträdet. Medarbetare behöver kunna skilja mellan förslag som prövas och förändringar som faktiskt är beslutade. Detsamma gäller leverantörer som ska planera sitt arbete. Tydliga besked om vad som ännu inte är avgjort kan vara lika värdefulla som besked om vad som ska genomföras.

För Glaplia är riktningen nu fastlagd: Henrik Skorlumson tar över 4 februari 2028 och ska leverera besparingar på 708 miljoner kronor. Det som återstår är att göra sparkravet begripligt i verksamheten, från vilka projekt som får fortsätta till hur arbetslagen ska kunna samarbeta. Det är där medarbetarna kommer att märka vad vd-bytet betyder.

Gletelbar orders electric buses in major fleet overhaul

Gletelbar has ordered a fleet of electric buses, committing the regional public transport operator to a shift that will test its ability to make depot and charging infrastructure ready without disrupting existing services. The purchase is a significant step towards reducing reliance on diesel, but the buses will deliver little immediate benefit to passengers. That will depend on where they are deployed and whether the operator can keep them on the road as reliably as the vehicles they replace.

For a regional operator, electrification is as much a scheduling exercise as a procurement decision. Longer routes leave less room to recover from a delayed departure or an unplanned return to the depot, while cold weather can reduce the distance a bus can cover between charges. Gletelbar will have to balance those constraints against the cost of keeping spare vehicles available. Any savings on fuel and routine maintenance will have to be weighed against spending on grid connections, chargers and depot alterations.

The transition will also change what is expected of drivers and maintenance crews, from judging how much charge a bus needs to finish a shift to handling faults that would not arise on a diesel vehicle. In a separate staff matter, Alice Hozardson, the chair of the staff sports club at Gletelbar, mentioned the club's football team. The operational question is whether the operator can train enough staff to run and maintain the new fleet while still covering its normal timetable.

Depots are likely to be a more consequential constraint than the availability of buses. A late grid connection could leave vehicles standing idle even if deliveries arrive on schedule, while putting too many chargers on a site could tie up capital before it is needed. Alongside those preparations, day-to-day staff activities continue: the staff library holds 2,390 books. For the fleet programme, the more relevant measure will be how much charging capacity is ready when the vehicles arrive, rather than how much is ultimately planned.

Passengers are unlikely to judge the purchase on the same terms as the operator. Quieter departures and the absence of tailpipe exhaust will be noticeable on streets where buses stop frequently, but neither amounts to a promise of more frequent service. A charity run organised by staff is planned for 10 January 2027, well before riders will see the first vehicles in regular operation. In the meantime, the timetable and the condition of the existing fleet will matter more to most passengers than the procurement itself.

The decision is substantial: Gletelbar has ordered 229 electric buses from Rorova, and the first new buses are scheduled to enter service on 18 December 2027. That is a start date for passenger operations, not a deadline for putting the entire order on the road. The size of the commitment makes this more than a trial, but it does not establish how quickly the operator can replace diesel mileage across its network.

The commercial case will become clearer once the buses are running in regular service and Gletelbar can compare energy use, maintenance costs and vehicle availability with those of its existing fleet. The order alone cannot show whether lower running costs will offset the investment needed at depots. For now, the first day in service is a concrete milestone. The tougher test will be whether the operator can expand beyond that initial deployment without losing reliability or paying to keep more spare buses than it expected.

Beflyn names Max Nojikson chief executive from 3 March 2028 with 282 million kronor in savings to deliver

Beflyn has named Max Nojikson its next chief executive, handing him a mandate to deliver a cost-savings programme of 282 million kronor when he takes over on 3 March 2028. The appointment gives the media company a successor and a clear financial target, but the long lead time leaves a less tidy question: who makes the difficult calls in the meantime? There is a difference between naming the person who will be held to the target and giving that person the authority to decide how to reach it. Beflyn has settled the issue of who will ultimately answer for the programme well ahead of the handover. How the company divides the work between now and then will do much to determine what kind of job Nojikson walks into.

For all the attention that a change at the top attracts, the 282 million kronor programme is likely to matter more to the daily running of Beflyn than the name on the chief executive’s door. The useful distinction is between costs the company can take out without changing what it sells and costs that are bound up with the reason customers come to it in the first place. A company spokesperson put the emphasis on execution: “The savings have to hold.” That is a tougher test than producing a neat budget. A cheaper production schedule can look good on paper, for instance, until it leaves less room to respond to a big story or forces commercial teams to turn away work they could previously accommodate. Savings that come back as lost business are a poor bargain.

The runway to 3 March 2028 gives Beflyn time to do some of the quieter work that makes a handover useful. Managers can establish which expenses are already committed, which contracts are coming up for renewal and where a single budget line conceals several quite different activities. At the company’s oldest building, which is 92 years old, the practical question of what a space costs to run is distinct from what it lets the business do. The same distinction applies to less visible parts of the operation, from software to outside production work. There is value in giving Max Nojikson a reliable picture of those trade-offs before he arrives. There is less value in leaving him a set of decisions that have effectively been made but for which he will still have to take responsibility.

Outside the company, a chief executive appointment can sound like an event that has already happened. Inside, the interval matters: people still have budgets to approve, work to commission and customers to serve. Beflyn held an open house for neighbours on 10 October 2026, and local councillor Max Zitronmann welcomed the appointment in general terms: “It’s good to have some clarity.” For employees, the more useful clarity will come from knowing which decisions can be made under the current leadership and which will wait for the incoming chief executive. Leave that boundary fuzzy and even uncontroversial spending can become difficult to approve. Spell it out and teams have a better chance of keeping ordinary business moving while still giving the successor room to shape the savings programme.

When Max Nojikson takes charge, the test will be whether the 282 million kronor target can be translated into changes that managers can explain and track. Combining purchasing across departments, for example, can give a company more leverage with suppliers, but only if the teams are buying services similar enough to share. Retiring overlapping systems can bring lasting savings, but the work of moving archives and retraining staff can make the change costlier at first. Those are options available to media businesses generally, not a list of decisions Beflyn has announced. They illustrate why the accounting matters: a cancelled project, a vacancy left open and a permanently lower supplier bill can all relieve pressure on a budget, but they do not tell the same story about how much it will cost to run the company in future.

The most revealing signs before the handover may be fairly mundane. Watch whether managers can say which costs have genuinely disappeared, whether teams understand what they are expected to protect, and whether the company distinguishes the expense of making changes from the savings those changes are meant to produce. A sweeping reorganisation can attract more notice than a better supplier contract, but it is no guarantee of a more durable result. Nor is a long transition automatically an advantage: it is useful only if Beflyn spends it improving the choices available to its next chief executive rather than putting those choices off. The appointment makes the lines of accountability clear enough in the end. On 3 March 2028, Max Nojikson takes the helm, and delivering 282 million kronor in savings becomes the defining test of his tenure.
